1.overview:
The LORD calls to Moses from the tent of meeting and begins with the burnt offering, the one sacrifice that goes up entirely in smoke. A worshiper who chooses to bring one may offer a male from the herd, a male sheep or goat, or a turtledove or young pigeon. With an animal, he lays his hand on its head, kills it, skins it, cuts it up, and washes the entrails and legs. Aaron's sons splash the blood around the altar, lay the pieces on the fire, and burn it all. A bird is handled by the priest alone.

Notice how much of the work belongs to the worshiper. He kills the animal himself, “before the LORD” (v. 5), and the priests take over where the blood meets the altar. Only one act is explained: the hand on the head, by which the animal “shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him” (v. 4).

1.hermeneutics:
After the Flood in the Babylonian Gilgamesh epic (tablet XI), Utnapishtim pours out offerings on a mountaintop. The gods smell the sweet savor and crowd around the sacrificer like flies, hungry after days without offerings. Genesis 8:21 uses the same idiom for Noah, and Leviticus 1 closes each of its three cases with it: “a sweet savour unto the LORD” (vv. 9, 13, 17). In Leviticus nobody gathers to eat. The whole animal goes up as smoke, and the phrase marks an offering the LORD accepts, whether it was a bull or a pigeon.

A Punic temple tariff found at Marseille, carved in the 3rd century BC and probably brought from Carthage, sets the fees owed to priests for each sacrifice. It runs down a ladder of victims: a whole ox, a calf or ram, a goat, a lamb or kid, and then birds. Its word for an animal offered entire, *kll*, matches Hebrew *kalil*, “whole burnt sacrifice” (Deuteronomy 33:10). Leviticus 1 follows the same descending ladder of herd, flock, and fowl, so a reader in the ancient world would recognize the menu. What is missing is the fee. Leviticus 1 sets no price for the priest and assigns him nothing; elsewhere he receives only the hide (7:8). The chapter is written for the one who brings the gift, not for the temple's accounts.

notes: **The refrain:** the Hebrew words for burnt offering, offering by fire, and soothing aroma stand together in vv. 9, 13, and 17, and the last two occur nowhere else in the chapter.
**Shrinking detail:** the herd case is told in full. The flock case drops the laying on of the hand, and in the bird case the priest does everything.

**Burning as smoke:** the verb behind “burn” in vv. 9, 13, 15, and 17 means to turn into smoke, the verb used for incense. When a sin-offering bull is burned outside the camp, a different verb is used (4:12, 21).

Exodus ends with the tent so full of glory that Moses “was not able to enter” (Exodus 40:35). Leviticus begins with the LORD calling him from inside it. That call opens one speech that runs to 3:17 and covers the gifts a worshiper brings by choice; a new speech at 4:1 turns to offerings required for sin.
**Forward:** Leviticus 6:8–13 returns to the burnt offering from the priests' side, with the fire that “shall never go out.”

traditions.text: Adam and Eve are commanded to offer the firstlings of their flocks long before Sinai. When an angel asks Adam why, he answers that the Lord commanded it, and the angel explains that the offering is “a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten of the Father.” The burnt offering of Leviticus 1 thus stands in a line that Restoration scripture traces back to the first family.

Amulek teaches that a great and last sacrifice is needed, one that is “neither of beast, neither of any manner of fowl.” Those are exactly the classes of Leviticus 1: herd and flock, then birds. He adds that the whole meaning of the law, every whit of it, points to that great and last sacrifice, the Son of God.

After the destruction at his death, the voice of Christ tells the survivors that their sacrifices and burnt offerings are done away. In their place they are to offer “a broken heart and a contrite spirit.” D&C 59:8 repeats the same sacrifice as a commandment for the latter days.

The midrash notices the first word of the book, “And he called.” Moses had led Israel out of Egypt and built the tabernacle, yet he did not enter the inner chamber until he was called. At the burning bush there was a pause between the call and the speech; at the tent there was none, which the rabbis compare to a king rejoicing among his household.

Verse 2 says “if any man,” using the Hebrew word *adam*. Rashi, following Leviticus Rabbah, reads it as a reminder of the first man: Adam owned everything, so he could never offer what was stolen. Neither may anyone who brings a burnt offering.

Philo calls the burnt offering the most excellent sacrifice, offered for the honor of God alone. He reads the hands laid on the victim's head as a sign of a blameless life: the worshiper should be able to say, “These hands have never received any gift as a bribe.” Washing the belly and feet stands for purified appetites and a soul that rises from the earth.

The Mishnah observes that the same phrase, a fire offering of pleasing aroma, is used for the animal (v. 9), the bird (v. 17), and the grain offering (2:2). It concludes that one who brings much and one who brings little are equal, provided the heart is directed to Heaven. Rashi repeats the point on v. 17.

Why must a bird be burned with its feathers (v. 17), when the smell would disgust anyone? Rabbi Yohanan answers: so that the altar is adorned with the poor man's offering. The midrash then tells of King Agrippa, who wanted his thousand burnt offerings to be the only sacrifices one day, and learned in a dream that a poor man's two turtledoves had gone before his.

Josephus describes the burnt offering as performed in his day: a bull, a lamb, or a kid, the last two in their first year, always male. The priests sprinkle the blood around the altar, cut the body into parts, salt them, and lay them on the burning wood, and the priests keep the hides. The salting applies the rule of Leviticus 2:13 to every offering.

A scribe agrees with Jesus that the two great commandments, love of God and of neighbor (Leviticus 19:18), are “more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” Jesus tells him he is not far from the kingdom of God. The comparison works because the whole burnt offering was the highest gift the altar knew.

Paul borrows the refrain of this chapter for Christ, who gave himself as a sacrifice “to God for a sweetsmelling savour.” He uses the same language for the Philippians' gift to him, an odour of a sweet smell. The altar phrase becomes a way to describe self-giving.

Aristotle's successor Theophrastus, in a passage Porphyry preserves, reports that the Jews do not feast on their victims. Instead, “having thrown the whole of the victims into the fire,” they pour honey and wine over them at night and consume them quickly. It is one of the earliest Greek descriptions of a whole burnt offering, though Leviticus 2:11 forbids honey on the altar; the night burning recalls Leviticus 6:9.

The Roman historian lists Jewish customs as deliberate reversals of Egyptian ones. “They slay the ram, seemingly in derision of Hammon,” he writes, and they sacrifice the ox because the Egyptians worship it as Apis. His explanation is hostile and his own, but it shows that the bull and the ram of the herd and flock were what outsiders knew of Israel's altar.

2.overview:
The grain offering comes next: fine flour with oil. A worshiper may bring the flour raw, with frankincense on top, or baked as cakes or wafers in an oven, on a flat pan, or in a frying pan. A priest takes a handful, with all the frankincense, and burns it on the altar as the “memorial.” Nothing burned on the altar may contain leaven or honey, every grain offering must be salted, and firstfruits come as ears of new grain roasted in the fire.

Notice where most of the gift ends up. Only a handful reaches the fire. The remainder belongs to Aaron and his sons and is called “a thing most holy” (vv. 3, 10), the first time Leviticus uses that phrase. With the grain offering, the altar begins to feed the men who serve at it.

2.hermeneutics:
Frankincense is the resin of trees that grow in southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, and it reached Israel by caravan. Jeremiah calls it “incense from Sheba,” brought “from a far country” (Jeremiah 6:20), and Isaiah pictures camels from Sheba bringing gold and incense (Isaiah 60:6). That makes the rule of vv. 2 and 16 pointed. The priest may keep most of the flour, but “all the frankincense” goes on the fire. The costliest, most foreign ingredient is the one part no one keeps.

Honey was a normal gift to the gods among Israel's neighbors. Hittite ritual texts use honey, written LÁL, to please and placate deities and set it on their offering tables. Leviticus bars honey and leaven from the altar fire (v. 11), yet in the next verse lets both come as firstfruits. Hezekiah's people bring honey among their firstfruits (2 Chronicles 31:5), and the firstfruit loaves of Pentecost are “baken with leaven” (23:17). The ban concerns what is burned, not the foods themselves.

Salt sealed obligations. Officials writing to the Persian king against Jerusalem say, in the Aramaic of Ezra 4:14, that they “eat the salt of the palace,” which the KJV renders “we have maintenance from the king's palace.” Sharing a king's salt bound them to him. Scripture speaks of a “covenant of salt” for the priests' portion (Numbers 18:19) and for David's line (2 Chronicles 13:5). Salt on every offering (v. 13) brings each gift under that kind of bond.

notes: **Frankincense** is named only in the frame (vv. 1, 2, 15, 16). The baked offerings in between have oil but no frankincense.
**Memorial:** the handful burned is called the memorial three times (vv. 2, 9, 16), once in each part of the chapter.
**Key word:** the Hebrew *minchah*, “gift,” occurs fifteen times in the chapter. The KJV renders it “meat offering,” meaning food in 1611 English; nothing in the chapter is flesh.
**Salt** is named three times in v. 13 alone.

Chapter 2 has no heading of its own. It sits inside the speech of 1:1–3:17, between the burnt offering and the peace offering, and chapter 3 carries on with “And if.” Like both neighbors, it ends its cases with a “sweet savour unto the LORD” (vv. 2, 9).
**Forward:** Leviticus 6:14–18 tells the priests how to eat their share, and 5:11–13 turns a plain handful of flour into a sin offering for the very poor.

traditions.text: Joseph Smith corrected the common assumption that ancient sacrifices were entirely burned. Leviticus shows, he said, that the priests offered a part as a memorial and kept the rest for their maintenance, so “the offerings and sacrifices are not all consumed upon the Alter.” The Joseph Smith Papers editors identify the passages as Leviticus 2:2–3, 9–10 and 5:12–13. He taught that these sacrifices would be restored when the temple is built and the sons of Levi purified.
traditions.cite: Instruction on Priesthood, c. 5 Oct. 1840, pp. 8–10 (Joseph Smith Papers)

traditions.text: Genesis 4 calls both Cain's produce and Abel's lamb a *minchah*, the word of this chapter, and gives no reason why only Abel's was accepted. Moses 5 supplies one: Cain “loved Satan more than God,” and he brought his fruit of the ground because Satan commanded him to make an offering. The fault lies in the giver; Leviticus 2 accepts grain as a most holy gift. In 1840 Joseph Smith said that Cain was authorized to offer sacrifice but did not offer it in righteousness.
traditions.cite: Moses 5:18–21; Genesis 4:3–5; Instruction on Priesthood, c. 5 Oct. 1840, p. 5

traditions.text: John the Baptist conferred the Aaronic Priesthood until the sons of Levi “offer again an offering unto the Lord in righteousness.” The words come from Malachi 3:3, where the Hebrew for “offering” is *minchah*, the word for this chapter's grain offering. In D&C 128 Joseph Smith quotes Malachi and calls on the Latter-day Saints to offer such an offering: a book of the records of their dead.

Verse 1 opens with the Hebrew *nefesh*, “soul,” where ch. 1 used “man.” Rabbi Yitzhak explains that a grain offering is usually the gift of a poor person. God says, in effect, that he will count it as if the poor man had offered his own soul. Rashi repeats the reading at the head of the chapter.

Why call it “the salt of the covenant” (v. 13)? Rashi reports that a covenant was made with salt during the six days of creation. The lower waters, separated from the heavens, were promised a place on the altar, as salt on every offering and as the water poured out at the Feast of Tabernacles.

Philo reads salt as a symbol of permanence, since it keeps bodies from decay. He offers two reasons for banning honey: bees were thought to arise from rotting oxen, and sweetness stands for pleasure that ends in pain. Leaven is excluded because it swells, and no one should approach the altar puffed up with pride.

The Mishnah rules that every grain offering is unleavened, with two exceptions: ten of the loaves brought with the thank offering and the two loaves of Shavuot. Both are found elsewhere in Leviticus (7:13; 23:17), and neither is burned on the altar. The exceptions fit the opening of v. 12, which allows firstfruits that are not burned.

Josephus describes a person who brings fine flour alone for a vow. The priest throws a handful on the altar as firstfruits and the priests eat the rest, boiled or mixed with oil and baked into cakes. A priest's own grain offering, he adds, must all be burned, following Leviticus 6:23.

Jesus' saying “every sacrifice shall be salted with salt” repeats the rule of v. 13, the only verse in the Law that makes salt a requirement of every offering. He sets it beside being salted with fire, a hard saying that follows warnings about the fire of hell. Then he turns it toward the disciples: salt is good, so they should have salt in themselves and peace with one another. The salt of the covenant becomes a quality of the disciples themselves.

This early church manual tells believers to gather on the Lord's day, break bread, and give thanks after confessing their sins, “that your sacrifice may be pure.” It grounds the rule in Malachi 1:11, where God promises a pure offering in every place. Malachi's word there is again *minchah*, so the Christian bread offering was read through the grain offering of Israel.

Irenaeus says Christ taught his disciples to offer God the firstfruits of creation. He did not need them, but they were not to be unfruitful or ungrateful. Christ took bread, gave thanks, and taught “the new oblation of the new covenant,” which Irenaeus identifies with Malachi's pure sacrifice. The KJV's word for the grain offering in vv. 4–7 is “oblation.”

3.overview:
The peace offering may come from the herd, the sheep, or the goats, male or female, as long as it is without blemish. As before, the worshiper lays his hand on its head and kills it at the door of the tent, and the priests splash the blood around the altar. Then the chapter turns precise: the fat over the entrails, the two kidneys with their fat, and the lobe above the liver are removed and burned, and from a sheep the whole fat tail as well. A closing rule reaches every home: Israel must eat neither fat nor blood.

Notice what the chapter leaves out. It lists only what goes to the altar and never says what becomes of the meat. That comes later (7:15–21, 31–34): the priest takes the breast and right shoulder, and the worshiper eats the rest. This is the one offering whose meat the giver himself eats.

3.hermeneutics:
Ritual texts from Ugarit on the Syrian coast (13th century BC) again and again pair two sacrifices: *šrp*, a burnt offering, and *šlmm*, a name from the same root as Hebrew *shelamim*, the peace offering. Leviticus 1 and 3 name a pair that Israel's neighbors already knew. What Leviticus adds is a precise division of the animal: the fat to the altar, the breast and shoulder to the priest, and the rest to the worshiper's table.

Greeks also gave the gods the fat. In Hesiod's *Theogony* (c. 700 BC), Prometheus divides an ox at Mecone, hiding the meat in the stomach and dressing the bones in shining fat for Zeus. Zeus chooses the fat, and Hesiod says this is why men burn white bones to the gods on fragrant altars. Leviticus 3 shares the custom but not the story of a trick. Fat is the choice portion, called “the food of the offering” (vv. 11, 16), and “all the fat is the LORD's.” The worshiper may not eat any of it (v. 17).

In Mesopotamia the sheep's liver was a book of omens. Thirty-two clay liver models from the palace at Mari, inscribed with omens, trained diviners to read its marks, and Ezekiel pictures the king of Babylon who “looked in the liver” (Ezekiel 21:21). Leviticus sends the lobe above the liver to the fire (vv. 4, 10, 15) and says nothing about examining it.

rows.text: Statute for all generations: no fat, no blood

notes: **Repeated list:** the inventory of fat, kidneys, and liver lobe is given three times almost word for word (vv. 3–4, 9–10, 14–15), so the reader learns it by heart.
**Key word:** the Hebrew *chelev*, “fat,” occurs twelve times. It builds to “all the fat is the LORD's” (v. 16) and the ban of v. 17.
**Food:** of chs. 1–3, only ch. 3 calls the altar portion *lechem*, “food” or “bread” (vv. 11, 16).

Chapter 3 closes the speech that began at 1:1 with three gifts a worshiper brings by choice. Each ends its cases with “a sweet savour” (3:5, 16). At 4:1 a new speech begins, and the subject shifts to offerings that sin requires.

**Backward and forward:** at Sinai young men “sacrificed peace offerings of oxen” to seal the covenant (Exodus 24:5). Leviticus 17:5 later requires that animals slaughtered in the open field be brought to the tent as peace offerings.

traditions.text: Moses 5 says Abel hearkened unto the voice of the Lord, and he brings the firstlings of his flock “and of the fat thereof.” The Lord has respect to his offering and not to Cain's. The fat that Leviticus 3 claims for the altar is already the choice gift in the first sacrifice scripture describes. Joseph Smith quoted the verse in 1840, arguing that sacrifices acceptable to God must be offered by those he has authorized, and that Abel magnified the priesthood he received.
traditions.cite: Moses 5:17, 20; Genesis 4:4; Instruction on Priesthood, c. 5 Oct. 1840, p. 4

traditions.text: Abinadi tells the priests of Noah that Israel was given “a law of performances and of ordinances,” to be kept strictly from day to day to keep them in remembrance of God. He adds that all these things were types of things to come. The detailed portions of Leviticus 3 belong to that law of daily remembrance.

Rashi gives two reasons for the name *shelamim*, from the word for peace. The offerings bring peace into the world. Or, following the Sifra, there is peace among all who share them: the altar receives the fat, the priests the breast and shoulder, and the owners the rest, so no one envies another.

Philo admits he has often wondered why the law takes the fat, the kidneys, and the liver lobe and not the heart or brain, where the mind lives. His answer is that the organ from which the mind went astray should not come to the altar of pardon. He adds that once the victim is offered it belongs to God, who makes the worshipers “partakers at the altar and messmates” at his own feast.

The Mishnah ranks peace offerings among the offerings of lesser holiness. They may be slaughtered anywhere in the temple court and eaten anywhere in Jerusalem, by any ritually pure person, cooked any way, for two days and the night between. The priests' share may be eaten by their wives, children, and servants.

The ban of v. 17 was taken with full seriousness. The Mishnah lists thirty-six offenses that carry *karet*, being cut off, when done on purpose, and eating forbidden fat and eating blood are both on the list. Leviticus 7:25 and 17:10 had already threatened the same penalty.

Josephus describes the thank offering of his day. The worshipers lay the kidneys, the caul, all the fat, the lobe of the liver, and the lamb's rump on the altar, and give the breast and right shoulder to the priests. They feast on the rest for two days and burn what remains.

Rabbis in the name of Rabbi Menahem of Galya taught that in the age to come every offering will cease except the thanksgiving offering, the joyful kind of peace offering (7:12). Likewise every prayer will cease except thanksgiving. They cite Jeremiah's promise that the sound of joy and of those bringing thank offerings will be heard again in Jerusalem.

Paul points to Israel's sacrificial meals: “are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar?” Eating a peace offering made the eater a sharer with the altar and with the God it belonged to, just as the meat on a pagan table bound its eaters to the idol. Paul draws the conclusion for the Lord's supper: a Christian cannot share the Lord's table and the table of devils.

The Jerusalem council asks Gentile believers to abstain, among other things, from blood and things strangled. The blood rule goes back to Genesis 9:4 and is repeated as a perpetual statute in v. 17 and in Leviticus 17:10–14. The fat rule of the same verse is not included, so the council kept half of the statute and set the other half aside for Gentiles.

Hebrews says Christians have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. It then names the offerings believers can bring: the sacrifice of praise, the fruit of their lips, and doing good and sharing. The thanksgiving offering, a kind of peace offering (Leviticus 7:12), lies behind the phrase.

Writing to Corinth about church order, Clement notes that the daily sacrifices, peace offerings, sin offerings, and trespass offerings were not offered just anywhere. They were brought only in Jerusalem, at the altar before the temple, after the high priest and ministers had examined the victim. He uses Leviticus as a model of worship done in its proper place and order.

4.overview:
A new speech turns from gifts to offerings that are required. When someone breaks one of the LORD's commands without meaning to, a sin offering is due, and the animal depends on who has sinned. The anointed priest and the whole congregation each bring a young bull, a ruler brings a male goat, and an ordinary Israelite brings a female goat or lamb. In every case the fat is burned as in the peace offering, the priest makes atonement, and “it shall be forgiven.”

Notice where the blood goes. For the priest and the congregation it is carried into the tent, sprinkled seven times before the veil, and put on the horns of the incense altar, and the rest of the bull is burned outside the camp. For a ruler or a commoner it goes only on the horns of the altar in the courtyard. The higher the sinner's standing, the deeper into the sanctuary his error reaches.

4.hermeneutics:
Mesopotamian prayers worry constantly about sins the worshiper cannot name. In a Babylonian penitential prayer the sufferer cries to “my god, whom I know and whom I know not,” and confesses that he did not know the sin he sinned or the transgression he committed. The incantation series *Šurpu* ends a long catalogue of possible offenses with the sin a man knows and the sin he does not know. Illness or misfortune came first; the sin was guessed at afterward. Leviticus 4 also deals with sin done “through ignorance” (vv. 2, 22, 27) and “hid from the eyes of the assembly” (v. 13). But the offering is brought when the sin “is known” (v. 14) or “come to his knowledge” (vv. 23, 28). The command broken is named, and there is no unknown god to placate.

Israelite altars had horns. Excavations at Tel Beersheba recovered a large altar of dressed stone with horns rising from its four top corners, found dismantled and built into a later wall; its excavator dated it to the 8th century BC, though the date is debated. The horns were the altar's most sacred points. Adonijah fled to the altar and “caught hold on the horns” for sanctuary (1 Kings 1:50), and once a year blood was put on the horns of the incense altar (Exodus 30:10). In Leviticus 4 blood is daubed on altar horns in every case (vv. 7, 18, 25, 30, 34), so each sin offering reaches the altar at its holiest point.

Congregation: bull, blood inside, burned outside the camp
Commoner: female goat or lamb, outer altar, “forgiven”

notes: **Forgiveness:** “it shall be forgiven” closes cases two to four (vv. 20, 26, 31, 35). The phrase never occurs in chs. 1–3; this chapter introduces it.
**One word, two meanings:** the Hebrew *chatta't* occurs twenty times and means both “sin” and “sin offering.” Verse 3 uses it both ways: he brings for his *chatta't* a bull for a *chatta't*.
**Telling shortens:** the priest's case is told in full. The congregation's case refers back to it (v. 20), and the last two cases say only what differs.
The heading at 4:1 opens the section on offerings that sin requires, running to 6:7. That is where Hebrew chapter 5 ends (5:26), and at 6:8 the speeches turn to instructions for the priests.

**Forward:** “the priest that is anointed” (vv. 3, 5, 16) is the first use in the Bible of *mashiach*, the word behind “Messiah.” Hebrews pictures Christ as a high priest who did not need to offer first for his own sins (Hebrews 7:27).

traditions.text: King Benjamin teaches that Christ's blood atones for those who died not knowing God's will “or who have ignorantly sinned.” The next verse marks the limit: woe to him who knows that he rebels against God, for he is saved only through repentance and faith in Christ. Leviticus 4 draws the same line between sins of ignorance and deliberate defiance (compare Numbers 15:27–30).

Amulek says no man can sacrifice his own blood to atone for the sins of another. The law, he says, was every whit pointing to the great and last sacrifice, after which the shedding of blood would stop. In Leviticus 4 a substitute's blood stands in for the sinner's; Amulek reads all such blood as pointing to Christ.

Who is the ruler, the *nasi*, of v. 22? The Mishnah answers that he is the king. The verse speaks of commands of “the LORD his God,” and only a king has no authority above him but God. Tractate Horayot builds its whole discussion on the cases of Leviticus 4: the anointed priest, the high court whose ruling misleads the congregation, and the king; a king or high priest who sinned before taking office brings only a commoner's offering.

The other cases begin with “if,” but the ruler's begins with *asher*, “when.” Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai heard in it *ashrei*, “happy”: happy is the generation whose king brings an offering for an unwitting sin. If the king does so, how much more will a commoner, and how much more will the king repent of sins done on purpose.

Philo explains the scale of victims. The nation outranks its ruler, since the whole is greater than the part, and the high priest is ranked with the whole nation because he serves it in prayer and sacrifice. He reads v. 3, a sin that brings guilt on the people, to mean that the true high priest stumbles only through the common errors of the nation. Such an error, he adds, easily admits of a remedy, which is what the bull of vv. 3–12 provides.

In the temple of the Mishnah, the bulls and goats that are burned are slaughtered on the north side of the court. Their blood is sprinkled on the curtain and on the golden altar, and the rest is poured at the western base of the outer altar. The carcasses are burned at the place of ashes outside Jerusalem, the city taking the place of the camp of v. 12.

Josephus summarizes the sin offering for one who sins in ignorance: a ewe lamb or a female kid, with the blood put on the corners of the altar and the fat, kidneys, and liver lobe burned. The priests eat the flesh in the holy place the same day, since the law does not let them leave any until morning. He says rulers bring a bull or a male kid, a little different from v. 23.

Hebrews observes that the bodies of animals whose blood the high priest brings into the sanctuary are burned outside the camp, as in vv. 12 and 21. Only these offerings, whose blood went inside, were treated so. Jesus, to sanctify the people with his own blood, likewise “suffered without the gate.” Believers are invited to go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach, since here they have no continuing city.

Hebrews says every high priest can have compassion on “the ignorant,” because he is himself beset with weakness and must offer for his own sins as well as the people's, as in v. 3. On the Day of Atonement he offers blood for himself and for the errors of the people. The Greek word for “errors” means sins of ignorance, the category of this chapter.

Paul writes that God made Christ to be sin for us, though he knew no sin. Augustine explains that under the old covenant “sacrifices for sin were called sins,” so Paul means that Christ was made a sacrifice for sin. The Hebrew of Leviticus 4 bears him out: *chatta't* names both the sin and the offering. Augustine adds that Christ was made sin in the same way that believers are made righteousness, not his own but ours.

5.overview:
Three everyday lapses call for a sin offering: staying silent after being put under oath as a witness, touching something unclean without realizing it, and swearing a rash oath and then forgetting it. The guilty person must confess and bring a female lamb or goat. If he cannot afford one, two birds will do, and if not even those, a tenth of an ephah of flour. A second speech (v. 14) brings in the trespass offering, a ram, for misusing something holy, with the value repaid plus a fifth, and for a wrong the person did not know he had done.

Notice the bottom of the scale. The poorest sinner brings plain flour, with no oil or frankincense, and the priest burns a handful of it. No blood is shed at all, yet the verdict matches the one given for the lamb: “it shall be forgiven him” (vv. 10, 13).

5.hermeneutics:
Ancient law treated the gods' property harshly. The Code of Hammurabi (18th century BC) puts to death anyone who steals the property of a temple or the palace (§6), and requires thirtyfold repayment for cattle or sheep belonging to a god (§8). Hittite instructions for temple personnel threaten death, without pardon, for a priest who parcels out a god's offering, and call it a capital sin when herdsmen swap the god's best animals and eat them. Leviticus 5:15–16 deals with the same offense, a trespass “in the holy things of the LORD,” but only when committed in ignorance. The penalty is the value plus a fifth and a ram, and “it shall be forgiven him.” Even deliberate fraud against a neighbor, once confessed, is settled the same way (6:1–7).

Israel had no coins before the Persian period. Silver was weighed against stone weights, and the ram of v. 15 is valued “by shekels of silver, after the shekel of the sanctuary.” Dome-shaped limestone weights from Judah, dated from the late 8th to the early 6th century BC, carry a shekel sign and numerals in Egyptian hieratic script, and work out to about 11.3 grams per shekel. Weights could vary from town to town and merchant to merchant, which is why a sanctuary standard mattered (Exodus 30:13 sets it at twenty gerahs). The ram's value was measured by a weight the merchant could not adjust.

notes: **Hidden:** the cases of vv. 2–4 each turn on something “hid from him,” a Hebrew verb used in those three verses.
**Confession:** v. 5 is the first time Leviticus requires a sinner to confess. The verb returns only twice more in the book, on the Day of Atonement (16:21) and in the promise of 26:40.
**Guilt in sevens:** the noun *asham*, “trespass offering,” and the verb “be guilty” from the same root each occur seven times in vv. 1–19.
**Forgiveness:** “it shall be forgiven him” closes each level of the scale and each ram (vv. 10, 13, 16, 18).

The KJV chapter break falls in the middle of a unit. Verses 1–13 finish the sin offering begun in ch. 4. Verse 14 opens the trespass offering, which continues through 6:7; in the Hebrew Bible those seven verses are 5:20–26, and chapter 6 begins only with the next speech.
**Forward:** Leviticus 7:1–7 adds the priests' rules for the trespass offering. Luke 2:24 shows Mary and Joseph using the two-bird allowance.

traditions.text: The Lord says that whoever has repented of his sins is forgiven, and that he remembers them no more. The sign of repentance is that a man “will confess them and forsake them.” Leviticus 5:5 makes confession the first step before any offering is brought.

On the Lord's day the Saints are told to offer their oblations and sacraments to the Most High, “confessing thy sins unto thy brethren, and before the Lord.” The KJV uses “oblation” for the offerings of Leviticus 2. As in v. 5, confession and offering go together.

After their conversion, the sons of Mosiah and Alma travel through the land “zealously striving to repair all the injuries” they had done to the church, confessing all their sins. Their repentance follows the pattern of the trespass offering in vv. 15–16 and 6:4–5: confession joined to repair of the harm done.

The Mishnah applies v. 1 to the oath of testimony. If a plaintiff asks two people to testify, they swear they know nothing, and they are later found to have lied, they owe the sliding-scale offering of vv. 6–13. Five oaths sworn outside the court make them liable five times; five sworn before the court count as one.

On the rash oath of v. 4 the rabbis debate how far “to do evil, or to do good” reaches. Their examples are everyday: an oath to sleep or not to sleep, or to throw a stone into the sea. Rabbi Yishmael limits the law to oaths about the future, as the verse's wording suggests, while Rabbi Akiva argues for a wider reading.

Verses 17–19 allow a ram for a sin a person is not sure he committed. Rabbi Eliezer says anyone may bring this provisional guilt offering any day, and it was called the guilt offering of the pious. Bava ben Buta reportedly brought one every day except the day after the Day of Atonement, and said he would have brought it then too if permitted.

The Mishnah works through the case that ends this unit (6:1–7). A robber who repays the principal but swears falsely that he has paid the fifth must treat that fifth as a new principal and add a fifth to it. The process repeats with each false oath until the amount owed is too small to matter, and a bailee who confesses a false oath pays principal and fifth and brings the ram.

Philo notes that an offense against holy things requires the value plus a fifth before the ram is offered. For the false oath of 6:1–7 he pictures a man who escapes his accusers but is “convicted by his own conscience residing within,” confesses, and repays. He concludes that the law treats an unintentional offense in holy things as equal to an intentional sin against men.

Josephus explains the trespass ram of vv. 17–19 differently from the rabbis. It is for a person who sins and knows it himself, though no one can prove it against him, and the priests eat the flesh in the holy place that day. Those who cannot afford a full sacrifice bring two pigeons or turtledoves.

At Jesus' presentation in the temple, Mary and Joseph offer “a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.” Luke quotes the purification law for mothers (Leviticus 12:8), which uses the same allowance for those who cannot afford a lamb that appears in v. 7. The detail places the holy family among the poor.

Jesus tells a worshiper who remembers at the altar that his brother has something against him to leave the gift and first be reconciled. Leviticus sets the same order for wrongs against a neighbor: repay the loss and the fifth, then bring the ram (6:4–6).
Verse 4 makes provision for a person who swears rashly and forgets the oath. Jesus goes further: swear not at all, by heaven, earth, Jerusalem, or one's own head. Let speech be simply yes or no.

Hebrews says that under the law “almost all things are by the law purged with blood,” and that without shedding of blood there is no remission. The flour of vv. 11–13, forgiven without any blood, is the kind of case the word “almost” leaves room for, though Hebrews does not name it.

6.overview:
The first seven verses finish the trespass offering. A man who lies to his neighbour about a deposit, a loan, a robbery, or something he found, and swears falsely to cover it, must give back the full amount plus a fifth and then bring a ram to the priest. From v. 8 the speech turns to Aaron and his sons. The altar fire must burn all night and never go out, and the priest clears its ashes in linen. The priests eat the grain offering and the sin offering inside the court, but the high priest’s own daily grain offering is burned whole.

Bibles divide this chapter in different places. Hebrew Bibles end chapter 5 with the trespass law, so KJV 6:1–7 is Hebrew 5:20–26, and Hebrew chapter 6 begins at the command to Aaron (KJV v. 8). The Hebrew break follows the change of audience from the people to the priests.

6.hermeneutics:
Babylonian law handled deposits with witnesses and oaths. The Laws of Hammurabi (18th century BC) tell a man to show what he deposits to a witness and draw up a contract; if he hands it over without them and the keeper denies it, he has no claim (§§122–123). Where nothing could be proved, the claim was settled by an oath before the god (§§120, 126), and Exodus 22:7–11 likewise brings such cases before the judges and an oath of the LORD. Leviticus 6:1–7 begins where those courts stop. The keeper has denied the deposit, sworn falsely, and got away with it; no witness or accuser is named. The case reopens only because the man himself is “guilty” and brings it forward (v. 4), and then the penalty is light: the principal plus a fifth, where a thief caught with the goods paid double (Exodus 22:7).

Temples elsewhere feared their fires. A Hittite text of the 14th or 13th century BC, the Instructions for Priests and Temple Personnel, warns the staff to be very careful with fire in the temple, and when night comes to put out whatever is left on the hearth with water. If carelessness let the temple burn, the guilty man died with his descendants. Leviticus 6 gives the opposite order three times in five verses: the fire burns all night (v. 9), it shall not be put out (v. 12), it shall never go out (v. 13). The risk was no smaller in a tent of wood and cloth. The difference lies in what the fire is: in Hatti a hearth to be doused for safety, in Israel the altar fire that keeps the LORD’s offerings burning day and night.

notes: **Four speeches:** “And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying” opens vv. 1, 8, 19 and 24. Only the first concerns the whole people; the other three tell the priests how to handle what the people bring.
**Headings:** “This is the law (*torah*) of…” introduces the burnt offering (v. 9), the grain offering (v. 14) and the sin offering (v. 25). The series runs on into ch. 7.

**Most holy:** the grain offering and the sin offering are each called “most holy” (vv. 17, 25, 29), and whatever touches them becomes holy (vv. 18, 27). Holiness behaves like something passed on by contact, so spattered garments are washed and the cooking pots broken or scoured (vv. 27–28).

Vv. 1–7 close the sin and trespass offerings of 4:1–6:7, spoken for the people. At v. 8 the same offerings are taken up again from the priests’ side: who eats what, where, and what stays on the altar. That second section runs to the summary in 7:37–38.

**Links:** The added fifth repeats the rule for trespass in the LORD’s holy things (5:16), so cheating a neighbour is priced like cheating the sanctuary. In 10:16–18 Moses applies v. 30 when the people’s sin-offering goat is burned instead of eaten.

traditions.text: D&C 59 tells the Saints to offer a sacrifice of a broken heart and a contrite spirit, and on the Lord’s day to bring their oblations “confessing thy sins unto thy brethren, and before the Lord.” Confession runs both ways, to people and to God. Vv. 1–7 make the same double move: the wrong is done to a neighbour and is also a trespass against the LORD, so the man repays the neighbour before he brings his ram.

In Moses 5 Adam offers the firstlings of his flocks long before Sinai, simply because he was commanded. An angel later explains that the offering is “a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten.” The burnt offering whose fire Leviticus 6 keeps alight is, in this account, the oldest form of worship, given to Adam and later regulated through Moses.

Rabbi Akiva asks why lying about a neighbour’s property is called a trespass “against the LORD” (v. 2). Loans and business, he says, are done before witnesses or with a document, but a man who leaves a deposit wants no one to know of it except the Third who stands between the two parties. Whoever denies the deposit therefore denies God, its only witness. Rashi quotes the saying on this verse.
traditions.cite: Sifra, Vayikra Dibbura deChovah 22:4; Rashi on Lev 5:21 (Hebrew numbering)

traditions.text: Philo describes the man of vv. 1–7 as one who has escaped his accusers and then becomes his own accuser, convicted by the conscience within him. Pardon is given, he says, to one who shows repentance by works rather than promises: returning the deposit or the stolen thing with the added fifth. Only after the injured man is appeased does he go to the temple with his ram. Philo and Rabbi Akiva both read the passage as a case no court could reach.

The Mishnah takes v. 5’s “give it unto him to whom it appertaineth” strictly. A man who robbed even a perutah, the smallest coin, and swore falsely must carry the payment with its fifth to the victim himself, even if he has gone as far as Media. He may not hand it to the victim’s son or agent, only to an agent of the court, and if the victim has died it goes to his heirs.

Clearing the ashes each morning (v. 10) was the first task of the priestly day. At first any priest who wanted it could do it, and when several did, they raced up the ramp of the altar. Once two arrived together, one pushed the other, who fell and broke his leg, so the court replaced the race with a daily lottery.

Among the wonders of the temple the Mishnah lists that rain never put out the fire on the wood pile. The Talmud adds a tradition that the altar fire crouched on the wood like a lion, while Rabbi Hanina, deputy high priest in the last years of the temple, said he saw it crouching like a dog. The answer given is that the lion was the First Temple’s fire and the dog the Second’s. Even when fire came from heaven, a priest still had to bring ordinary fire (Leviticus 1:7).

A letter at the start of 2 Maccabees says that when Judah went into exile, devout priests hid the fire of the altar in a dry pit. Generations later Nehemiah sent their descendants for it; they found only “thick water,” which he had sprinkled on the wood and the sacrifices, and when the sun came out a great fire blazed up. The story assumes vv. 12–13: the altar fire was meant to be continuous, not lit anew.

The high priest’s grain offering of vv. 19–23 was baked from a tenth of an ephah he brought from his own house, half offered in the morning and half in the evening. If he died after the morning half, his successor had to bring a whole new tenth and half of each was lost. If no successor was yet appointed, Rabbi Shimon said the community paid for it and Rabbi Yehuda said his heirs did.

Jesus tells a worshipper who remembers at the altar that his brother has something against him to leave his gift there, “first be reconciled to thy brother,” and then come back and offer it. The order is the order of vv. 5–6, where the man repays his neighbour before he brings his ram, and the one Philo stresses.

V. 30 forbids eating any sin offering whose blood is brought into the sanctuary; it is burned instead. Hebrews builds on that rule: the bodies of those beasts are burned outside the camp, so those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat from the Christian altar. Jesus, it says, likewise suffered outside the gate.

7.overview:
The instructions to the priests continue. The trespass offering is handled like the sin offering, and the priest who makes atonement with it eats it (vv. 1–7). The skin of a burnt offering and most grain offerings also go to the priests (vv. 8–10). Then comes the peace offering, the one sacrifice ordinary Israelites ate themselves. A thanksgiving offering, brought with loaves, is eaten the same day; a vow or freewill offering may last into the second day; anything left on the third day is burned (vv. 11–21). Israel may eat no fat and no blood (vv. 22–27). The breast and right shoulder of every peace offering belong to the priests (vv. 28–36), and a summary closes the laws of offering (vv. 37–38).

The thread running through the chapter is who eats what. Every animal is divided three ways, between the altar, the priests, and the worshipper’s own table.

7.hermeneutics:
Israel’s neighbours had names for some of the same offerings. Ritual texts from Ugarit on the Syrian coast (13th century BC) list *šlmm*, from the root of Hebrew *shelamim* (peace offerings), together with burnt offerings, and they share Israel’s words for altar and temple. Yet, as Richard Hess sums up Dennis Pardee’s edition of those texts, they never mention expiation, sin, atonement, blood, or fat. Those are exactly the concerns of Leviticus 7. The chapter reserves the fat for the altar (vv. 3–5, 31), forbids Israel to eat fat or blood at all (vv. 23–27), and ties the priest’s share to the atonement he makes (v. 7). The Ugaritic lists record what was offered to which god; Leviticus also says what each part means and who may eat it.

Temples had to feed their staff, and the priests’ cut was a matter for written rules. The Marseille Tariff, a Punic inscription of the 3rd century BC probably carried from Carthage, sets the silver fee and the share of meat the priests receive for each animal and each kind of offering, including the *kll*, the same word as the “wholly burnt” offering of 6:22–23. It ends by fining any priest who takes more than the inscription allows. Herodotus says Egyptian priests received beef and geese from the temple every day (Histories 2.37). Leviticus 7 fixes Israel’s tariff in the same way: the skin, the grain offerings, the breast and the right shoulder, “by a statute for ever” (vv. 8–10, 34). Eli’s sons later broke such a rule by taking raw meat before the fat was burned (1 Samuel 2:13–16).

notes: **The law of…:** the Hebrew *torah* (“law, instruction”) occurs seven times in 6:8–7:38 (6:9, 14, 25; 7:1, 7, 11, 37). Six are headings or the summary; in v. 7 the sin and trespass offerings share “one law.”
**Cut off:** “that soul shall be cut off from his people” comes four times (vv. 20, 21, 25, 27): twice for eating holy meat while unclean, twice for eating fat or blood.
**One extra item:** the summary lists “the consecrations” (v. 37), an offering not described in chs. 1–7. It points ahead to the ram of consecration in 8:22–29.

Vv. 37–38 close the priests’ instructions begun at 6:8 and the whole block of offerings opened at 1:1. The summary places these laws “in mount Sinai,” in the day Israel was commanded to bring its offerings. With ch. 8 the book turns from law to narrative.

**Links:** The breast and shoulder of the peace offerings become food for Aaron’s whole household, daughters included, in 10:14–15. The “sacrifice of thanksgiving” is the offering the psalms call for (Psalms 50:14; 107:22).

traditions.text: Abinadi tells the priests of King Noah that Israel was given a very strict law because it was slow to remember God. He calls it “a law of performances and of ordinances,” to be kept from day to day to keep them in remembrance of God and their duty. All these things, he says, were types of things to come, though many did not understand that salvation comes only through the redemption of God.

Nephi writes that his people believe in Christ and still keep the law of Moses until it is fulfilled. The law has become “dead unto us,” he says, yet they keep it because it is commanded. Alma 25 describes converted Lamanites keeping the same outward performances while looking forward to Christ. In this account the offerings of chs. 1–7 were still practiced in the Americas until Christ came.

After giving the sacrament to the Nephites, Jesus forbids his disciples to let anyone knowingly partake of his flesh and blood unworthily, for whoever does so eats and drinks damnation to his soul. The concern runs parallel to vv. 20–21, where an unclean person who eats the peace offering is cut off. Paul makes the same point to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 11:27–29).

The Mishnah sets the time limits of vv. 15–16 in practice. The thanksgiving offering is eaten anywhere in Jerusalem by any clean person, on its day and the following night until midnight, while an ordinary peace offering lasts two days and the night between. The priests’ share of both may be eaten by their wives, children and slaves.

V. 12 names three kinds of unleavened bread and v. 13 adds leavened bread. The Mishnah counts ten loaves of each kind, forty loaves for every thanksgiving offering, baked from twenty tenths of an ephah of flour. So large a meal had to be shared to be eaten in a day.

Several rabbis say in the name of Rabbi Menahem of Galya that in the age to come every offering will cease except the thanksgiving offering, and every prayer except the prayer of thanks. They cite Jeremiah 33:11, where the restored city hears voices of praise and those who bring “the sacrifice of praise into the house of the LORD.” The thanksgiving offering of v. 12 outlasts all the rest.

Philo gives several reasons the peace offering must be eaten within two days. Meat kept longer spoils; the sacrifice belongs to God, so it should be set out for anyone in need, not hoarded; and the two days answer to the two things preserved, soul and body. The thanksgiving offering is limited to one day so that those who receive God’s gifts freely may repay without delay.

Josephus summarizes these rules for Greek readers. In the thank-offering the kidneys, caul, fat and lobe of the liver go on the altar; the breast and right shoulder go to the priests; and the offerers feast on the rest for two days and burn what remains. He adds that the priests receive the hides of burnt offerings, as v. 8 directs.

Resh Lakish reads v. 37, “This is the law of the burnt offering, of the meat offering…”, to mean that anyone who studies Torah is credited as though he had offered every one of them. Rava reads it more strongly: whoever studies Torah needs no burnt, grain, sin or trespass offering. After the temple fell, the summary verse became a charter for study in place of sacrifice.

Clement of Rome, urging order in the Corinthian church, points to the temple. The continual daily sacrifices, the freewill offerings, the sin offerings and the trespass offerings are not offered everywhere, he writes, but only in Jerusalem, before the sanctuary, by the high priest and ministers, after the victim is inspected for blemishes. Each order of priest and layman has its own appointed service.

Paul uses the priests’ portions to argue that ministers may live from their ministry: those who wait at the altar are partakers with the altar. Earlier in the letter he points to Israel eating its sacrifices as a sign of fellowship with the altar, which is the logic of the peace offering’s shared meal.

Hebrews closes by naming a sacrifice Christians still offer: “the sacrifice of praise to God continually,” which it explains as the fruit of lips giving thanks. The Hebrew word for the thanksgiving offering of v. 12, *todah*, also means praise and thanks. Leviticus Rabbah makes the same offering the one that never ends.

8.overview:
Moses carries out the ordination commanded in Exodus 29. With the whole congregation gathered at the tent door, he washes Aaron and his sons, dresses Aaron in the high priest’s garments, and anoints the tabernacle, the altar, and Aaron’s head. Three animals follow: a bull for a sin offering, a ram for a burnt offering, and the ram of consecration, whose blood he puts on each priest’s right ear, thumb, and big toe. He sprinkles oil and blood on the priests and their garments, and they eat the meat and bread at the door. They are to stay there seven days.

Moses, not Aaron, is the officiant. Until the seven days are over Aaron is not yet a priest, so Moses slaughters, burns, and waves, and even takes the breast of the consecration ram as his own portion (v. 29). Only the last verse hands the work on: Aaron and his sons did everything commanded “by the hand of Moses.”

8.hermeneutics:
Priests across the ancient world were marked first by washing and clean clothing. Herodotus, who visited Egypt in the 5th century BC, reports that its priests shaved the whole body every other day, wore a single linen garment, and washed in cold water twice by day and twice by night (Histories 2.37). Leviticus 8 also begins with water and clothes. Before oil or blood touches him, Aaron is washed at the tent door and dressed (vv. 6–9), and his coat and breeches are linen (Exodus 28:39, 42). Here, though, the washing is done once, by Moses, in front of the assembled people. What Herodotus describes as a priest’s daily discipline becomes the public first act of an installation.

Anointing a priest is rare in the surviving texts. Anointing appears in Near Eastern legal and political settings, and one Amarna letter (EA 51) has a pharaoh anoint a Syrian vassal. The closest priestly parallel is a ritual from Emar in Syria (14th–12th century BC). Emar 369 installs the high priestess of the storm god: on the first day fine oil from the palace and from a temple is put on her head, and on the second day oil is poured on her head again at the god’s gate, in a ceremony of about nine days. Leviticus 8 shares the head-anointing and the rite spread over days, but it divides the oil. It is poured on Aaron’s head alone (v. 12), while his sons are only sprinkled with oil mixed with blood (v. 30). The anointing marks the high priest off from the priests who serve with him.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, each stage closed by a note of obedience.

rows.text: “Moses did as the LORD commanded him”

notes: **Seven notes of obedience:** “as the LORD commanded Moses” closes five stages (vv. 9, 13, 17, 21, 29). With v. 4 (“as the LORD commanded him”) and v. 36 (“by the hand of Moses”), the chapter reports obedience seven times. The verb “command” occurs 11 times in all.
**Sevens in the rite:** the word “seven” occurs four times. Moses sprinkles the altar seven times (v. 11), and the priests stay at the door seven days (vv. 33, 35).
**Contrast ahead:** the refrain sets up 10:1, where Nadab and Abihu offer fire “which he commanded them not.”

Chs. 8–10 turn law into narrative: offerings described in chs. 1–7 are now performed for the first time. Ch. 8 covers the seven days of 8:33, ch. 9 the eighth day, and the unit 8:1–9:24 closes when fire from the LORD consumes the offerings.
**Links:** The rite carries out Exodus 29 almost line by line. The same three marks of blood on ear, thumb and toe cleanse a healed leper (Leviticus 14:14).

traditions.text: Joseph Smith records that John the Baptist conferred the Priesthood of Aaron on him and Oliver Cowdery and told them to baptize each other. Afterward each laid hands on the other and ordained him to the Aaronic Priesthood, “for so we were commanded.” As in Leviticus 8, the order of acts is set by command, and the priesthood is received from one already authorized.

The Lord tells the Saints at Nauvoo that he commanded Moses to build a tabernacle so that ordinances hidden from before the world might be revealed. He lists their “anointings, and your washings” among the ordinances of his holy house, together with memorials for sacrifices by the sons of Levi. Washing and anointing, the opening acts of Leviticus 8, are named as temple ordinances.

Rashi, following the Sifra, reads “Take Aaron” (v. 2) as “win him over with words,” since Aaron had to be persuaded to accept the office. On v. 3, where the whole congregation gathers at the tent door, he cites Leviticus Rabbah: this is one of the places where a small space held a great multitude. On v. 15 he explains that Moses purified the altar of anything unfit so it could enter holiness.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Lev 8:2–3, 15; Sifra, Mekhilta deMiluim; Leviticus Rabbah 10:9

traditions.text: V. 34 says that as Moses had done that day, “so the LORD hath commanded to do, to make an atonement.” The rabbis took “to do” as the burning of the red heifer (Numbers 19) and the atonement as the Day of Atonement. From this verse they derived that the high priest, and the priest who burned the heifer, were set apart from their homes for seven days beforehand, as Aaron was kept at the tent door.
traditions.cite: Sifra, Mekhilta deMiluim 1:37, cited by Rashi on Lev 8:34; Yoma 2a, 3b

traditions.text: Philo gives each animal a meaning. The bull is offered for remission of sins because to sin is congenital to every created being, however good. The first ram is a burnt offering of gratitude for the ordered world, and the second, which he calls the “ram of perfection,” completes the priests’ purification. In the oil mixed with blood (v. 30) he sees the priests sharing both the purity of the open court and that of the inner shrine.

A baraita in the name of Rabbi Yehuda says many miracles were done with the anointing oil Moses made. Only twelve log were prepared, yet the tabernacle, its vessels, Aaron and his sons were anointed with it through all seven days, high priests and kings were anointed with it for generations, and the whole amount remains for the age to come. The baraita quotes v. 10.

The Mishnah marks this chapter as a turning point in Israel’s worship. Until the tabernacle was set up, private altars were allowed and the firstborn performed the service; once it was set up, private altars were forbidden and the service passed to the priests. Ordination ends the old arrangement.

Josephus says Moses sprinkled Aaron, his garments and his sons with the blood of the slain beasts and purified them with spring water and ointment, and so they became God’s priests. He did this for seven days, and the same to the tabernacle and its vessels with oil and with the blood of bulls and rams slain day by day. Josephus treats the whole week as a repeated rite, where Leviticus describes it in detail only once.

Hebrews says Moses sprinkled “both the tabernacle, and all the vessels of the ministry” with blood, and that under the law almost everything is purged with blood. Leviticus 8 anoints the tabernacle with oil and puts blood on the altar, and Hebrews draws the general rule: without shedding of blood there is no remission.

Hebrews contrasts Aaron’s line with Christ. The law, it says, makes high priests who have infirmity, while the word of the oath makes the Son, “who is consecrated for evermore.” The seven days of consecration in Leviticus 8 had to be repeated for every new high priest; Hebrews describes a consecration that never needs repeating.

Explaining the anointing that followed baptism in his church, Tertullian traces it to the old practice of anointing men with oil from a horn when they entered the priesthood, “ever since Aaron was anointed by Moses.” Aaron was called christ, anointed, from the chrism, and the name passed to the Lord, anointed with the Spirit. Cyril of Jerusalem later makes the same link.

9.overview:
On the eighth day Aaron serves at the altar for the first time. Moses tells him to offer a calf and a ram for himself, and the people to bring their own offerings, “for to day the LORD will appear unto you” (v. 4). Aaron offers his own sin offering and burnt offering, his sons bringing him the blood, and then the people’s offerings. He lifts his hand toward the people and blesses them. Moses and Aaron go into the tent, come out, and bless the people again. Fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the offering on the altar, and the people shout and fall on their faces.

The order matters. Every offering is complete by v. 21, but the LORD’s answer comes only after the blessing and the entry into the tent. The fire does not light a cold altar; it falls on offerings already burning there (vv. 13, 17).

9.hermeneutics:
Mesopotamian texts describe the gods as clothed in an overwhelming radiance, Akkadian *melammu*, often paired with *puluhtu*, fear. Temples could be said to wear it, and a god could grant it to a king as a mark of his rule (A. Leo Oppenheim, 1943; Shawn Zelig Aster, 2012). Israel’s word for the visible splendour of God is *kavod*, “glory,” and Leviticus 9 builds toward its appearing. The people’s response matches the old pairing of radiance and dread: they shout and fall on their faces (v. 24). The difference is where the glory shows itself. It rests on no statue in a shrine; it appears “unto all the people” (v. 23) over an altar where a sin offering has just been made for them.

Blessing and prayer went with a raised hand. Babylonian scribes even named a class of prayers after the gesture: the *šu-ila*, “lifting of the hand.” Aaron “lifted up his hand toward the people, and blessed them” (v. 22), turning a gesture usually aimed at a god toward the congregation. Leviticus does not give his words, but Numbers 6:22–27 assigns a fixed blessing to Aaron and his sons, and that blessing is old. Two small silver scrolls found in a tomb at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, dated to the late 7th or early 6th century BC, carry a text very close to Numbers 6:24–26. They were rolled up and probably worn as amulets, a sign of how much the priestly blessing was valued by ordinary people.

structure.summary: Inclusio: the promise that the LORD will appear (vv. 4, 6) is fulfilled when his glory appears (v. 23).

open.text: “To day the LORD will appear unto you”

close.text: The glory of the LORD appears; fire consumes the offering

notes: **Appear and see:** the Hebrew verb *ra’ah* occurs four times. The LORD “will appear” (vv. 4, 6), his glory “appeared” (v. 23), and the people “saw” the fire (v. 24). *Kavod*, “glory,” occurs only in vv. 6 and 23.
**Commanded:** the verb occurs five times (vv. 5, 6, 7, 10, 21). In v. 21 the subject is Moses: Aaron waves the portions “as Moses commanded.”
**Priest first:** Aaron’s offerings come before the people’s, in the same order, sin offering then burnt offering (vv. 8–14, 15–16).

Ch. 9 closes the ordination unit (8:1–9:24). The seven days at the door end with the eighth day, and the fire from before the LORD answers everything done since 8:1. The opening words of 9:24 return in 10:2, where the same fire kills Nadab and Abihu.
**Backward:** Exodus 40:34–35 ends with the glory filling the tabernacle so that Moses cannot go in. Here Moses and Aaron go in together, and the glory appears to all the people.

traditions.text: Conferring the Priesthood of Aaron on Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery, John the Baptist said it would never be taken from the earth until the sons of Levi “offer again an offering unto the Lord in righteousness.” The words echo Malachi 3:3, where the refiner purifies the sons of Levi so that they may offer in righteousness. Leviticus 9 is the first time the sons of Levi in Aaron’s line offer at all.

In an essay on priesthood read at a conference in Nauvoo, Joseph Smith quoted Malachi 3 and taught that sacrifice was not done away. The offering of sacrifice, he wrote, “forms a part of the duties of the priesthood” and has always been connected with it, and these ordinances will be continued when the priesthood is restored. He tied this to Elijah, who held the keys to administer all its ordinances.
traditions.cite: Instruction on Priesthood, c. 5 Oct. 1840, pp. 8–9 (Joseph Smith Papers)

traditions.text: At the dedication of the Kirtland Temple, Joseph Smith prayed that the Lord’s glory would rest on his people and on the house they dedicated. A week later he and Oliver Cowdery saw the Lord in the temple, who declared, “I have accepted this house.” Leviticus 9 ends the same way, with a sanctuary completed, a blessing given, and the LORD’s glory appearing as a sign of acceptance.

Speaking from the darkness after his death, the Lord tells the Nephites that their sacrifices and burnt offerings are done away and that he will accept none of them. In their place they are to offer a broken heart and a contrite spirit, and he will baptize such people “with fire and with the Holy Ghost.” The fire that once fell on the altar is now promised to the offerer.

A baraita says the day the tabernacle was raised “took ten crowns.” It was the first day of creation’s week, the first day of the princes’ offerings, the first of the priesthood, the first of service, the first descent of fire, the first eating of holy food, the first resting of the Divine Presence, the first priestly blessing of Israel, the first day private altars were forbidden, and the first of the months. Rashi identifies that day with the eighth day of this chapter.

Why did Moses and Aaron go into the tent (v. 23)? One answer is that Moses taught Aaron the incense service. Another is that when every offering was done and no fire had come, Aaron was ashamed and said the LORD must be angry with him; Moses went in with him, they prayed, and the Divine Presence came down. Moses had told the people that through Aaron’s service they would know their sin with the golden calf was forgiven.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Lev 9:23; Sifra, Mekhilta deMiluim 2:18

traditions.text: Philo says that on the eighth day Moses led his brother into the tabernacle and taught him, like a teacher with a pupil, how the high priest should minister within. When they came out and raised their hands in prayer for the nation, a body of flame burst from the inmost shrine and fell on the altar. Whether it was pure ether or air turned to fire, he says, it showed that nothing done there happened without God’s providence.

Josephus says that on the eighth day Moses made a feast for the people, who competed with one another in the sacrifices they brought. As the sacrifices lay on the altar, a fire kindled from among them “of its own accord,” looking like a flash of lightning, and consumed everything on the altar. Philo has the fire come from the shrine; Josephus has it rise from the offerings.

The letter in 2 Maccabees sets this scene beside the temple’s dedication: as when Moses prayed, the fire came down from heaven and consumed the sacrifices, so Solomon prayed and fire came down. The next line remembers Moses saying that the sin offering was consumed because it was not to be eaten, a memory of the dispute in 10:16–20.

Hebrews says every high priest taken from among men must offer for sins “as for the people, so also for himself,” because he too is beset with weakness. That is the order of vv. 7–15, where Aaron’s calf comes before the people’s goat. Hebrews then sets Christ apart as a high priest who has no need to offer first for his own sins.

10.overview:
On the day the priests begin to serve, Aaron’s two eldest sons, Nadab and Abihu, put fire and incense in their censers and offer “strange fire before the LORD, which he commanded them not” (v. 1). Fire comes out from the LORD and kills them. Moses quotes the LORD, “I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me,” and Aaron says nothing. Two cousins carry the bodies out, and Aaron and his remaining sons may neither mourn nor leave the tent. The LORD then tells Aaron that priests must drink no wine on duty and must teach the difference between holy and common. The chapter ends with Moses angry that the people’s sin-offering goat was burned, and with Aaron’s reply, which satisfies him.

The text never says what made the fire strange. It says only that the LORD had not commanded it, after two chapters that stress, again and again, everything the LORD commanded.

10.hermeneutics:
Temple service in the ancient Near East was dangerous for the staff. The Hittite Instructions for Priests and Temple Personnel (14th or 13th century BC) set death as the penalty for misusing the god’s offerings, and they argue from a master’s anger: if someone angers a god, does the god punish him alone? No, the text answers, but his wife, children, descendants and servants as well. Leviticus 10 shares the fear of wrath spreading. Aaron and his sons must not mourn “lest wrath come upon all the people” (v. 6). Yet here the fire takes only the two who offered, and the survivors are told exactly what to do to live.

Grief had standard gestures. In the Baal cycle from Ugarit, the high god El mourns Baal by coming down from his throne, pouring dust on his head, putting on sackcloth and gashing his skin. Israelite mourners let their hair hang loose (KJV “uncover”) and tore their clothes, the two acts forbidden to Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar in v. 6, because the anointing oil is on them (v. 7). The whole house of Israel may bewail the burning; the priests on duty may not. Leviticus 21:10–12 later makes the rule permanent for the high priest.

Some Egyptian priests also kept wine away from their god. Plutarch (*Isis and Osiris* 6, c. AD 100) reports that the priests of Heliopolis brought no wine at all into the shrine and that other priests drank it only in great moderation. The ban in vv. 8–11 is narrower and tied to a task: no wine or strong drink when entering the tent, so the priests can tell holy from common and clean from unclean, and teach Israel the statutes.

notes: **Same fire:** the opening words of v. 2 repeat 9:24 exactly in Hebrew: “there went out fire from (before) the LORD and devoured.” The fire that accepted the offering now consumes the men who offered unbidden.
**Die:** the verb *mut* occurs four times (vv. 2, 6, 7, 9). After the deaths of v. 2, each use is a warning to the survivors: “lest ye die.”
**Aaron alone:** v. 8 is the only place in Leviticus where the LORD speaks to Aaron without Moses. The silent Aaron of v. 3 is the one addressed, and in v. 19 he is the one who answers Moses.

Ch. 10 stands between the ordination (8–9) and the purity laws, which begin in ch. 11 with a new speech to Moses and Aaron. Both scenes fall on the same day and ask what priests may and may not do near holy things. The charge to distinguish “between unclean and clean” (v. 10) introduces chs. 11–15.
**Forward:** Leviticus 16:1 opens the Day of Atonement “after the death of the two sons of Aaron,” and its rules for entering the most holy place answer what happened here.

traditions.text: D&C 84 promises that “the sons of Moses and also the sons of Aaron” will offer an acceptable offering and sacrifice in a house of the Lord to be built in that generation, and will be filled with the glory of the Lord. Those who obtain the two priesthoods and magnify their callings, it says, become the sons of Moses and of Aaron. Leviticus 10 turns on an offering the LORD had not commanded and on Aaron’s question whether his would have been accepted (v. 19).

The rabbis disagreed about the sin. Rabbi Eliezer said Nadab and Abihu died because they gave a legal ruling in the presence of their teacher Moses. Rabbi Ishmael said they entered the sanctuary drunk, and pointed to the ban on wine that follows at once (vv. 8–9).
traditions.cite: Rashi on Lev 10:2; Sifra, Mekhilta deMiluim 2:32; Eruvin 63a; Leviticus Rabbah 12:1

traditions.text: A tradition in the name of Rabbi Levi counts four causes, each tied to a verse that threatens death: they had drunk wine, they lacked the full vestments, they had not washed hands and feet, and they had no children (Numbers 3:4). Abba Hanin adds that they had no wives. Others say they were arrogant, thought no woman good enough for them, and asked when the two old men, Moses and Aaron, would die so they could lead.

Moses’ words in v. 3 point back to Exodus 29:43, where the tabernacle is “sanctified by my glory.” The rabbis reread “my glory” as my honoured ones, and have Moses tell Aaron that he knew the house would be sanctified through those closest to God, and had expected it to be one of them; now he saw that Aaron’s sons were greater than both. Aaron’s silence was rewarded: the next word of the LORD came to him alone (v. 8).
traditions.cite: Zevachim 115b; Leviticus Rabbah 12:2; Rashi on Lev 10:3

traditions.text: Discussing execution by burning, the Talmud notes a view that Nadab and Abihu died by a burning of the soul while their bodies stayed intact. The text itself supports something like it: their cousins carried them out “in their coats” (v. 5).

Philo reads the deaths as a passage to life. Nadab and Abihu “die in order that they may live,” exchanging mortal life for immortal, for no dead man can come into the sight of the Lord. Elsewhere he says Moses forbids mourning for them because they were taken up by unquenchable fire and imperishable light, consumed like a whole burnt offering.
traditions.cite: On Flight and Finding 59; On Dreams 2.67

traditions.text: Josephus says the two elder sons did not bring the sacrifices Moses commanded but those they had used before, and were burned to death by a fire no one could quench. Moses had their father and brothers carry them out of the camp and bury them with honour, and the people mourned them. He presents Aaron as bearing the blow with firmness, already dressed in his sacred garments.

The Sifra explains Moses’ anger in v. 16 by counting three goats offered that day: the people’s sin offering of 9:3, the goat brought by Nahshon at the dedication of the altar, and the goat for the new moon. Only the new-moon goat was burned. Some said it had touched something unclean, others that the priests, as mourners, held back only from the offering ordained for all generations. Moses was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the Sifra adds, out of respect for Aaron.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Lev 10:16; Sifra, Shemini 2; Zevachim 101a

traditions.text: On v. 20, “when Moses heard that, he was content,” Rashi says Moses admitted his error and was not ashamed to do so. He did not claim he had never heard the rule; he said he had heard it and forgotten. Here the lawgiver is corrected by the high priest he has just ordained.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Lev 10:20; Sifra, Shemini 2:12; Zevachim 101b

traditions.text: After describing the temple’s ordered offerings, Clement warns the Corinthians that those who act contrary to the seemly ordinance of God’s will “receive death as the penalty.” Greater knowledge, he adds, brings greater danger. He applies the lesson of Leviticus 10, priests dying for unauthorized service, to disorder among church leaders.

Writing against schism, Cyprian lists those punished for claiming priestly power God had not given: Korah, Dathan and Abiram, King Uzziah with his censer, and “the sons of Aaron, who placed strange fire upon the altar.” He reads strange fire as worship offered outside God’s appointed order, and Clement makes a similar point.
traditions.cite: On the Unity of the Church 18

11.overview:
The LORD tells Moses and Aaron which animals Israel may eat. Land animals must both part the hoof and chew the cud, which rules out the camel, the coney, the hare, and the swine. Water creatures need fins and scales. Twenty kinds of birds are named as forbidden, and of the winged insects only four kinds of locust may be eaten. The rest of the chapter turns to touch: whoever touches or carries a carcass is unclean until evening, and a dead swarming creature that falls into a pot or onto an oven makes it unclean.

Notice where the chapter lands. After the hooves, fins, and carcasses, verses 44–45 give the reason: “ye shall be holy; for I am holy.” It is the first time Leviticus tells the people to be holy, and it ties what Israel eats to the God who brought them up out of Egypt.

historicalContext.text: The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron together (v. 1), as again in 13:1, 14:33, and 15:1. The rules are for all “the children of Israel” (v. 2), not for priests alone.

11.hermeneutics:
Food rules were common in the ancient Near East, but most belonged to priests or to the service of a particular god. Herodotus, who visited Egypt in the 5th century BC, reports that Egyptian priests could not eat fish and would not even look at beans. He adds that Egyptians held the pig unclean: a man who brushed against one went and dipped himself in the river, clothes and all, and swineherds were barred from every temple. Leviticus 11 has touch rules too, but it gives its list to “the children of Israel” as a whole (v. 2). A whole nation keeps a table that elsewhere only temple staff kept, which fits the chapter's closing call for the people to be holy.

Archaeology adds a second angle. The small Iron Age villages in the hill country, where Israel first appears, have yielded almost no pig bones, while the Philistine cities on the coast, such as Ekron and Ashkelon, have them in quantity. Scholars debate how much of that gap comes from identity and how much from herding conditions in the hills. Either way, avoiding pork was visible in Israel's world very early. Leviticus itself gives the pig no special place. It is one of four border cases (vv. 4–7), each of which has one sign of a clean animal and lacks the other.
