notes: **Creation's categories:** The groups follow the living things of Genesis 1: beasts of the earth, creatures of the waters, fowl, and creeping things. The Genesis phrase “after his kind” occurs 9 times here.
**Repetition to watch:** The Hebrew root for “unclean” (*tame*) occurs 34 times, and “abomination” (*sheqets* and its verb) 11 times. “Until the even” comes 9 times, all in vv. 24–40.
**The turn at the end:** “Holy” occurs 4 times, all in vv. 44–45. The closing verse then uses the verb “make a difference” (*lehavdil*), the same word 10:10 used for the priests' task.

Chapters 11–15 are the book's section on clean and unclean. Leviticus 10:10 charges the priests to “put difference between holy and unholy, and between unclean and clean,” and these chapters supply the rules: food, childbirth, skin disease, and bodily discharges. Each part ends with a summary line beginning “This is the law,” which occurs 8 times in chs. 11–15, first at v. 46.

**Later echoes:** Leviticus 20:25–26 returns to clean and unclean animals as the sign that God has set Israel apart. Ezekiel's restored temple gives the priests the same duty, to teach the people to discern “between the unclean and the clean” (Ezekiel 44:23).

traditions.text: Where Jesus teaches that nothing entering a man from outside can defile him, the Joseph Smith Translation adds the words “which is food.” What defiles, it says, is what proceeds “forth out of the heart.” The revision makes plain that the saying concerns food, the subject of this chapter (see Acts 10 and Mark 7 below).

Given to missionaries sent to preach to the Shakers, this revelation says that whoever forbids people to eat meat “is not ordained of God.” The beasts of the field and the fowls of the air were made for man's food and clothing, and for abundance. The wording draws on 1 Timothy 4:3–4, which calls every creature of God good.

The Word of Wisdom also governs what Latter-day Saints eat and drink, but it is a different kind of law. Leviticus sorts animals into clean and unclean and grounds the rule in holiness (vv. 44–45). D&C 89 draws no such line; it ordains the flesh of beasts and fowls for man's use “with thanksgiving,” to be eaten sparingly, and promises health and wisdom to those who keep its sayings.

A Greek-speaking Jewish writer has the high priest Eleazar explain the food laws to curious foreigners. Moses did not legislate out of concern for “mice and weasels,” he says; the rules teach righteousness. The permitted birds are tame grain-eaters and the forbidden ones are birds of prey, a lesson against violence, while the animal that chews the cud stands for memory. Philo and Barnabas later read the signs in similar ways.

During the persecution under Antiochus IV, Eleazar, an aged scribe, was forced to open his mouth to eat swine's flesh. He spat it out and went to his death rather than live “stained with such an abomination.” Daniel 1:8 tells an earlier story of a young Jew who would not defile himself with the king's food.

Philo says Moses banned the animals whose meat tempts most, naming pork as the richest land meat and scaleless fish as the most delicate, to train Israel in self-control. He reads the two signs as lessons. Chewing the cud is a student turning over what he has learned until it is fixed in memory, and the parted hoof is the power to tell the road to virtue from the road to vice.

Reads the four animals of vv. 4–7 as the kingdoms that ruled Israel: the camel is Babylon, the coney Media, the hare Greece, and the pig Edom, the rabbis' name for Rome. The pig, it says, stretches out its cloven hooves when it lies down as if to say “See that I am pure,” the way Rome made a show of justice while it robbed. The scheme follows the four beasts of Daniel 7, which the same passage cites.

The rabbis ask how a traveler in the wilderness can tell a clean animal whose hooves have been cut off. One answer is its teeth: an animal without upper front teeth chews the cud, provided it is not a young camel. On the pig, the school of Rabbi Ishmael reasons that the Ruler of the world knows no other animal parts the hoof and is still unclean, which is why the verse singles it out.

Peter, praying on a rooftop, sees a sheet let down holding four-footed beasts, creeping things, and fowls, and is told to kill and eat. He protests that he has never eaten anything common or unclean, and the voice answers, “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.” Peter takes the vision to mean he should call no man unclean (10:28), and he goes to the Gentile Cornelius. Earlier, Mark 7:19 had reported Jesus' teaching on food in words the King James Version renders “purging all meats.”

Barnabas says Moses gave the food laws “in a spiritual sense,” but Israel took them as rules about eating. The swine stands for people who forget the Lord when they are full and cry out to him only when hungry. Chewing the cud is meditating on the word, and the parted hoof is the righteous man who walks in this world while looking to the holy world to come. His reading runs close to Aristeas and Philo.

The Roman presbyter argues that the unclean animals cannot be unclean in themselves, since God called everything he made “very good” and kept these creatures alive in Noah's ark. The law is spiritual (Romans 7:14), he says, and in the forbidden animals it pictures the habits of men that should be shunned.

The Roman historian offers an outsider's explanation in his account of Jewish origins. Jews abstain from swine's flesh, he says, in memory of the leprosy they once suffered, a disease to which the pig is liable. The idea grows out of hostile Egyptian and Greek stories of Israel as a band of lepers driven out of Egypt, stories Josephus wrote to refute.

12.overview:
A woman who gives birth to a son is unclean for seven days, as in her monthly separation, and on the eighth day the boy is circumcised. She then continues thirty-three days “in the blood of her purifying,” touching no hallowed thing and staying away from the sanctuary. For a daughter both periods double, to fourteen days and sixty-six. When the days are over she brings a lamb for a burnt offering and a pigeon or turtledove for a sin offering, or two birds if she cannot afford a lamb.

Notice the arithmetic. Seven and thirty-three make forty days for a son; fourteen and sixty-six make eighty for a daughter. The text never explains why the time doubles for a girl, and readers from Jubilees to the Talmud offered their own reasons.

12.hermeneutics:
Egypt also set a span of days after birth before a mother returned to ordinary life. In a story from the Westcar Papyrus, Ruddedet gives birth to three sons who are to become kings, and then she “purified herself with a fourteen days' purification” before she sends her maid to see whether the house is ready. The story treats the days as routine. Leviticus 12 has the same kind of waiting period, but it measures something else. The mother's household life is not in view. What she may not do is touch a hallowed thing or enter the sanctuary (v. 4), so the days mark her distance from the holy, and an offering at the tabernacle ends them.

Circumcision was older than Israel and widespread. Herodotus says the Egyptians practiced it “for cleanliness' sake,” and a relief in the tomb of Ankhmahor at Saqqara, from about 2300 BC, shows priests circumcising youths, not infants. Among Israel's neighbors it seems to have marked puberty or marriage, which is how Genesis 34 can make it a condition for the men of Shechem. Leviticus 12:3, following Genesis 17:12, moves it to the eighth day of life. Here the rite falls on the day after the mother's first seven days end, so the son enters the covenant as she passes into her second stage.

notes: **The son's panel is longer:** Only it includes the circumcision on the eighth day (v. 3), set between the seven days and the thirty-three.

**Matching words:** Each panel compares the mother's state to her monthly “separation” (*niddah*), the word's only two uses in the chapter (vv. 2, 5). Each also has “purifying,” which occurs 4 times in all (vv. 4, 5, 6).

**A summary, then a postscript:** “This is the law” closes the chapter at v. 7. Verse 8 follows it with the cheaper offering for a mother who cannot afford a lamb, the same concession 5:7 makes for other offerings.

The shortest section of the purity laws stands between the animals of ch. 11 and the skin disease of chs. 13–14. Its opening ties it forward to ch. 15: the mother's first stage is “according to the days of the separation for her infirmity,” the monthly rule spelled out in 15:19–24. Like the other sections, it closes with “This is the law” (v. 7).
**Links:** Circumcision on the eighth day goes back to the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:12), and Luke 2:21 records it for Jesus.

traditions.text: In the Joseph Smith Translation, God gives Abraham the covenant of circumcision so that he may know that “children are not accountable before me until they are eight years old.” Read with it, the eighth-day rite of v. 3 points to the age of accountability, which D&C 68:27 also sets as the age of baptism.

Explains a dispute in the apostles' day: unbelieving husbands wanted their children circumcised and brought under the law of Moses, following a tradition that held little children unholy. The revelation answers that little children are holy, “sanctified through the atonement of Jesus Christ.” Mormon tells his son the same, adding that in Christ the law of circumcision is done away.

Jubilees finds the origin of this law in Eden. Adam was created in the first week and Eve shown to him in the second, so a mother is unclean seven days for a son and twice seven for a daughter. Adam was brought into the garden after forty days and Eve after eighty, because the garden is holier than all the earth, and so a mother may enter the sanctuary only after forty or eighty days.

In his summary of the law, Josephus says a mother may not come into the temple or touch the sacrifices for forty days after bearing a boy, and twice that number after a girl. When the time is over she offers her sacrifices, which the priests distribute before God. He counts the days as one span and does not mention the two stages, nor the cheaper offering of birds for the poor.

The rabbis tie the forty and eighty days to the forming of the child. A miscarriage within forty days of conception, they rule, does not count as a birth, since nothing had yet formed. Rabbi Ishmael holds that a male is complete on the forty-first day and a female on the eighty-first, while the majority set both at forty-one. Aristotle (below) worked with similar numbers.

Opens its reading of the chapter with Psalm 139:5, “thou hast beset me behind and before,” taken as God shaping a person from first to last. It then asks why the law of childbirth comes right after the law of animals. Rabbi Simlai answers that man was created after the beasts, cattle, and birds, so his law is written after theirs: 11:46 closes the law of the animals, and 12:2 opens the law of a woman who has given birth.

Students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai asked why the law sets seven days for a son and fourteen for a daughter. In the pain of labor, he said, a woman vows to keep away from her husband; everyone rejoices over a son, so she regrets the vow after seven days, but after a daughter only after fourteen. Circumcision waits until the eighth day so that the parents are not still kept apart while everyone else celebrates.

When the days of her purification were fulfilled, Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the temple and offered “a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.” That is the offering v. 8 allows a mother who cannot afford a lamb. Luke mentions the law five times in the scene, and Paul writes that Christ was born of a woman under the law (Galatians 4:4).

Asked by Augustine of Canterbury how soon a mother might enter church after giving birth, the pope answered that the thirty-three and sixty-six days are to be taken “in a mystery.” If she comes in the very hour of delivery to give thanks she commits no sin, and to forbid her would make a crime of her pain. He also allowed a mother or her newborn to be baptized in the very hour of birth if death threatened. Bede preserved the exchange in his history of the English church.

The Greek philosopher records that a male child usually first stirs in the womb around the fortieth day and a female around the ninetieth, adding that there are many exceptions. Like the rabbis' forty-one and eighty-one days, it ties a boy and a girl to different spans of time, though Leviticus itself gives no reason for its numbers.

13.overview:
Anyone with a swelling, a scab, or a bright spot on the skin is brought to the priest, who looks for two signs: hair in the spot turned white, and a spot deeper than the skin. If the signs are clear he pronounces the person unclean. If not, he shuts the person up for seven days and looks again. The same test is applied to old sores, healed boils, burns, the scalp and beard, and bald heads. Whoever is declared unclean tears his clothes, covers his upper lip, cries “Unclean, unclean,” and lives alone outside the camp. The chapter closes with the same plague in wool, linen, and leather.

Notice what the priest does not do. He gives no remedy and names no cause. He looks, waits, and declares, and the question he settles is who may live in the camp around the sanctuary.

13.hermeneutics:
Skin disease was a stock curse in Assyria. The succession treaty that Esarhaddon imposed on his vassals in 672 BC calls on the moon god Sin to “clothe you with leprosy,” to bar the oath-breaker from the presence of the gods and the king, and to send him to roam the desert like the wild ass and the gazelle. The disease meant being cut off from temple, palace, and town. Leviticus 13 has the same result: the unclean person lives alone, outside the camp (v. 46). What it leaves out is the curse. The chapter never says who sent the disease or why, and the priest passes no judgment on the person's sins.

A medical text from Emar in Syria, copied in the 13th century BC, sorts the same kind of disease by color (white, yellow, red, black) and gives a remedy for each, such as an anointing repeated for seven days. Leviticus 13 also sorts by color, as well as by depth, hair, and spread, and it works in periods of seven days. It gives no remedy at all. The priest is a judge of the signs, and healing is left out of his hands.

The English word “leprosy” came through Greek. The Septuagint rendered the Hebrew *tsara'at* as *lepra*, a Greek medical term for scaly skin conditions; the disease now called leprosy, Hansen's disease, the Greeks called *elephantiasis*. The signs listed here fit it poorly: spots that clear in a week or two, hair turned white, a body white from head to foot declared clean (v. 13), and the same word used for a growth on cloth. The Hebrew names a visible blemish that makes a person or thing unclean, wider than any one disease.

notes: **One procedure, many cases:** Each case runs the same course. A sign appears, the priest looks, and he either declares the person clean or unclean or shuts him up for seven days. “Shut up” occurs 9 times.
**Repetition to watch:** “Priest” occurs 56 times and the verb “see” or “look” 32 times, so the chapter is built around the priest's eyes. The Hebrew *tsara'at* occurs 21 times.
**Person, then cloth:** The rules for the unclean person's life (vv. 45–46) close the human cases. Verses 47–58 then apply the same tests to garments, as 14:33–53 will to houses.

Chapters 13–14 form one unit, closed by the summary in 14:54–57, which lists every case in both chapters: skin, garment, and house. Chapter 13 diagnoses; chapter 14 gives the rite for a person who has healed and adds the rules for houses.

**Links:** Miriam is shut out of the camp for seven days when she becomes leprous (Numbers 12:10–15), and King Uzziah, struck while burning incense, lives in a separate house until his death (2 Chronicles 26:19–21).

traditions.text: At the temple in Bountiful the risen Jesus asks the Nephites to bring their sick, the lame and the blind, “or leprous,” and all who are afflicted, and he heals every one. He does it, he says, because they desire to see what he had done for their brethren at Jerusalem, where the Gospels record lepers cleansed (Luke 17, below). Where Leviticus 13 can only declare, this account heals.

This Qumran text, which recasts the Torah's laws for an ideal temple city, requires three separate places east of the city: one for lepers, one for those with a discharge, and one for men who have had an emission of seed. It carries the camp rule of v. 46 over to the holy city and keeps apart the groups that chs. 13–15 treat one after another.

Philo is struck by the rule that a person white from head to foot is clean, while a patch of raw, living flesh makes him unclean (vv. 12–15). Usually the sick defile the healthy, he notes, but here healthy flesh defiles. He reads it of the soul: the living flesh is conscience, which convicts deliberate sin, while wrongs done without intent, however widespread, carry no blame.

Josephus says the law kept lepers out of the city and away from others, “as if they were in effect dead persons.” He then answers writers who claimed Moses was himself a leper who led lepers out of Egypt. A leper, he argues, would never have made laws so much to his own dishonor, and in many nations lepers held high office and entered temples. Moses, he concludes, was free of the disease and made these laws for the honor of God.

Anyone who knows the signs may examine a mark on the skin, the Mishnah rules, but only a priest may declare it clean or unclean. The expert tells the priest, “Say: unclean,” and the priest repeats the word. Two marks may not be examined at the same time. The same tractate exempts non-Jews from these laws, and Kelim counts walled cities as holier ground because lepers must be sent out of them.

The rabbis link this disease with evil speech, and Deuteronomy 24:8–9 already pairs the plague with Miriam, who was struck after speaking against Moses. Rabbi Yohanan lists seven sins that bring the plague, starting with slander, and a related teaching says the bells on the high priest's robe atoned for evil speech, sound for sound. Another sage explains why the leper must “dwell alone” (v. 46): by his talk he separated husband from wife and friend from friend, so he is set apart.

Ten lepers meet Jesus at the edge of a village and, as v. 46 requires, stand “afar off” and call to him. He sends them to show themselves to the priests, the judges of the disease under this chapter, and they are cleansed on the way. Only one turns back to give thanks, a Samaritan, and Jesus asks where the other nine are, calling the man who returned a “stranger.”

Marcion held that Jesus broke the Old Testament law by touching a leper. Tertullian answers that the rule against touching the leper was a figure for avoiding sinners, and that Christ, being God, could not be defiled by contact. He adds that Elisha cleansed only Naaman of all the lepers in Israel (Luke 4:27), a sign of the nations to be cleansed in Christ.

Among the Persians, Herodotus reports, a citizen with leprosy or “the white sickness” may not come into town or mix with other Persians, because they say he has sinned against the sun. Many drive foreigners with the disease out of the country, and white doves with them. The exclusion matches v. 46; the explanation, a sin against a god, is the part Leviticus leaves unsaid.

An Egyptian priest who wrote his country's history in Greek, Manetho told of a king who sent eighty thousand lepers and other impure people to the quarries. Their leader was a priest of Heliopolis named Osarsiph, who, Manetho says, forbade them to worship Egypt's gods and later changed his name to Moses. Josephus preserves the story only to refute it, pointing to Moses' own laws on leprosy.

14.overview:
When a skin disease has healed, the priest goes outside the camp to confirm it. One bird is killed over running water, and a living bird is dipped in its blood with cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop; the priest sprinkles the healed person seven times and lets the living bird fly off into the open field. After washing, shaving, and seven more days, the person brings lambs on the eighth day, and the priest puts blood and oil on the right ear, right thumb, and right big toe. A poor person may bring one lamb and two birds. The chapter ends with houses in Canaan that show greenish or reddish streaks.

Notice the ear, thumb, and toe. The same three marks were put on Aaron and his sons at their ordination (Exodus 29:20). The rite that brings an outcast back into the camp borrows the gestures that set apart a priest.

14.hermeneutics:
A medical text from Emar in Syria, copied in the 13th century BC, ends its treatment of a skin disease of this kind with a rite for the patient who has recovered. One partridge is burned before the sun god Shamash, and in the reading of the scholar Yitzhaq Feder a second partridge is wiped over the patient's body and then let go, carrying the disease away. Leviticus 14 has the same pair: one bird killed, one released “into the open field” (v. 7). The difference is in what surrounds it. Emar gives incantations and remedies for the illness itself; Leviticus keeps only the rite after healing, addressed to no power but the LORD, and moves on to offerings at the tabernacle door.

In Mesopotamia a fungus on a house wall was an omen. The twelfth tablet of the omen series *Šumma ālu* is devoted to it: black fungus promised success, while white, red, or green meant calamity, and its place on the wall told which member of the household would die. A ritual of the *namburbi* type, meant to turn aside a bad omen, had a priest inspect the growth, scrape it off, and dispose of it. Leviticus 14:33–53 follows the same steps of inspection, scraping, and removal for “greenish or reddish” streaks (v. 37). It reads no fate in them. The priest even has the house emptied before he goes in (v. 36), so that its contents are not made unclean.

**Same rite, smaller gift:** The poor man's version repeats the blood and oil on ear, thumb, and toe step by step; “ear” occurs 4 times (vv. 14, 17, 25, 28). Only the animals change.
**Atonement:** “Make an atonement” (*kipper*) occurs 7 times, the last of them for the house (v. 53).

The summary in vv. 54–57 closes the unit begun at 13:1. It lists the cases in the order of the two chapters, with garments and houses squeezed in at v. 55. The law of houses (vv. 33–53) opens with a new speech to Moses and Aaron, and it is the one part of the purity laws set in Canaan: the unclean stones go “without the city,” where ch. 13 spoke of the camp.
**Links:** Cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop return in the ashes of the red heifer (Numbers 19:6), and hyssop dipped in blood first appears at the Passover (Exodus 12:22).

traditions.text: The rabbis spell out the rite of vv. 4–7. A new clay flask holds a quarter-log of spring water, the slain bird is buried in front of the healed person, and the cedar, hyssop, and scarlet are tied together with the tips of the living bird's wings and tail, then dipped and sprinkled seven times on the back of his hand. The living bird is released facing neither the sea, nor the city, nor the wilderness, since v. 53 says “into the open fields.”

On v. 35 the rabbis note the owner's careful wording: even a learned sage who is sure of what he sees must tell the priest only that there is “something like a plague” in his house. Houses of non-Jews are exempt, and so are round or triangular houses and houses built on a ship. The priest shuts the house up from its doorway, never from inside, and the new stones may not be taken from another wall of the same house.

Why must the healed person bring birds? Because the disease comes for evil speech, which is a kind of chatter, so the cleansing uses birds that chatter all day. Rashi carries the reading through the other items. The tall cedar answers pride, and the scarlet, dyed with a worm, and the low hyssop teach the healed person to make himself lowly.

Opens its reading of the chapter with the seven things the LORD hates in Proverbs 6:16–19 and says all of them are punished with this disease. It then tells of a peddler in Sepphoris who cried, “Who wants the elixir of life?” and showed his buyers Psalm 34:12–13: whoever desires life must keep his tongue from evil. The word play the rabbis heard in *metsora*, the leper, and *motsi ra*, one who spreads evil, runs through the whole section.

Rabbi Hiyya asks how a plague in a house can be good news, when v. 34 announces it as God's gift. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explains that the Canaanites hid their gold in their houses when they heard Israel was coming, but God had promised Israel houses full of all good things (Deuteronomy 6:11). God sends the plague, the owner tears down the wall, and he finds the treasure. Rashi repeats the story on v. 34.

traditions.text: One teaching holds that a house struck with this plague never existed and never will, and that the law was written so that people could study it and be rewarded. It ties this view to a sage who required the mark, the size of two split beans, to appear on two stones in two walls meeting at a corner. Two other sages disagree from experience. Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Tzadok knew a ruin near Gaza called the leprous ruin, and Rabbi Shimon of Akko saw a place marked off where such stones had been thrown.

A leper kneels to Jesus and begs to be made clean, and Jesus, moved with compassion, touches him and heals him at once. He then sends the man to show himself to the priest and offer for his cleansing “those things which Moses commanded,” the offerings of this chapter, as a testimony to them. All three Synoptic Gospels keep the instruction, and Luke 17 sends ten lepers to the priests in the same way.

Preaching on Matthew 8, Chrysostom says that Jesus' hand was not made unclean by the leper; rather the leprous body was made clean by his hand. Why then send the man to the priest? Jesus did the healing himself but left the approving of it to the priests, making them judges of his own miracle, so that no one could call him a breaker of the law and their own verdict would testify against them if they refused to believe.

Hebrews describes Moses sealing the covenant at Sinai with blood, water, scarlet wool, and hyssop. Exodus 24 mentions only blood; the full set of items is the one this chapter's bird rite uses together (vv. 4–6, 51–52). The writer draws the general rule that under the law almost all things are purged with blood, and that “without shedding of blood is no remission,” then turns to the blood of Christ.

15.overview:
A man with a running discharge is unclean, and so is anything he lies on, sits on, or rides on. Whoever touches him or those things washes his clothes, bathes, and is unclean until evening. When the discharge stops he counts seven days, bathes in running water, and on the eighth day brings two birds to the priest. An emission of seed, or a man and woman lying together, calls for bathing and leaves both unclean until evening. A woman's monthly flow makes her unclean for seven days, and a flow of blood beyond that time is treated like the man's discharge, ending with seven clean days and two birds.

Notice the closing reason. These rules matter, v. 31 says, so that Israel does not die by defiling “my tabernacle that is among them.” The concern is the sanctuary in the middle of the camp, which every household lived near.

15.hermeneutics:
Egypt and Greece also kept sex apart from sacred space. Herodotus says the Egyptians were the first to make it a religious rule not to lie with women in temples, nor to enter a temple after intercourse without washing, and he counts the Greeks as equally careful. Leviticus 15:16–18 asks the same washing of every Israelite, man and woman, and adds a wait until evening. The concern is the one Herodotus names, contact with holy space. In Israel, though, the holy space is a tent in the middle of the camp, so the rule reaches every household and not only those who go up to a temple.

Workmen's records from Egypt show these matters in ordinary life. A limestone register from Deir el-Medina, the village of the royal tomb builders, dated to Year 40 of Ramesses II (about 1250 BC), notes why each of forty men missed work on given days. Some entries give a wife or daughter “bleeding,” usually read as menstruation. Whatever kept the man at home, the woman's monthly period was a known part of the household's routine and could change a man's day. Leviticus treats it in the same household terms. It governs beds and seats and those who touch them (vv. 20–23), and it lasts seven days.

structure.summary: Chiasm (A B C B′ A′) centered on v. 18, as Wenham and Whitekettle have noted, followed by a closing reason and summary.

close.text: That they die not in their uncleanness

notes: **The center:** Verse 18 is the only case that involves both a man and a woman, and it sits between the man's cases and the woman's.

**The outer pairs:** The two abnormal, long-lasting discharges (A, A′) each end with seven clean days and two birds, a sin offering and a burnt offering (vv. 15, 30). The two ordinary events (B, B′) need only washing and time.
**Repetition to watch:** “Until the even” occurs 15 times, and the Hebrew verb for “be unclean” 25 times. “Bathe” comes 12 times and “wash” (of clothes) 11 times.

Chapter 15 ends the purity laws of chs. 11–15 with a summary of its own cases (vv. 32–33). Chapter 16 follows directly. The uncleanness these chapters keep away from the sanctuary is cleansed once a year on the Day of Atonement, when the high priest atones for the holy place “because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel” (16:16).
**Links:** Leviticus 12:2 measures a new mother's first days by the monthly rule of vv. 19–24, and Deuteronomy 23:10–11 applies the evening washing of v. 16 to the war camp.

traditions.text: The LDS edition's footnote to v. 31 points to D&C 94:9, a revelation about a house of the Lord: if any unclean thing comes into it, his glory and presence will not be there. D&C 97 promises that the pure in heart who come into such a house “shall see God,” and the Kirtland Temple dedicatory prayer asks that no unclean thing be permitted to pollute it. The same footnote cites Moses 6:57, where no unclean thing can dwell in God's presence.

On the rule against relations during the monthly period (v. 24; 18:19), Philo says a husband must respect the laws of nature. A man who ignores them is like a farmer who, drunk or out of his mind, sows wheat in a flooded marsh instead of a dry field. Nature cleanses the womb each month, he says, and the husband should wait for the proper season like a skilled farmer.

Josephus says men with a discharge were kept out of the city, and women in their monthly period were kept apart until the seventh day, when they were counted pure and let back in. A man with an emission in his sleep went down into cold water and was then like a husband lawfully with his wife. Elsewhere he explains the washing of v. 18: a defilement is contracted in soul and body, “as if they had gone into another country.”

Before a man is declared to have the discharge of vv. 2–15, the Mishnah has him examined seven ways: what he ate and drank, what he carried, whether he had jumped or been ill, and what he had seen or thought. Any of these might explain a single discharge without making him unclean. When Rabbi Akiva wanted to count any food at all, the sages protested that there would then be no such cases, and he answered that they were not responsible for there being any.

The Mishnah ranks the holy places in rings. Men and women with discharges, women in their monthly period, and new mothers may not enter the Temple Mount. Gentiles and those defiled by a corpse may go no farther than the rampart just inside it, and a person who has bathed but awaits sunset may not enter the Court of Women, and one still owing the offering for his cleansing (vv. 14–15, 29–30) may not enter the Court of Israel. The rings set in stone the concern of v. 31 for the sanctuary.

Rabbi Meir gives the seven days of v. 19 a reason that has nothing to do with the sanctuary. A husband who could always be with his wife would tire of her, he says, so the Torah sets seven days apart, after which she is as dear to him as on the day she entered the wedding canopy. It is one of many rabbinic attempts to explain a law that Leviticus leaves unexplained.

A woman with an issue of blood for twelve years, unclean under vv. 25–27 the whole time, has spent all she had on physicians and grown worse. She comes up behind Jesus in a crowd, touches his garment, and is healed at once. Jesus does not rebuke her for the touch; he calls her “Daughter” and sends her away in peace. Matthew and Luke tell the same story.

Asked whether women in their monthly period may enter the house of God, the bishop of Alexandria thought the question needless. Pious women, he wrote, would not presume in that state to approach the holy table or touch the body and blood of the Lord, just as the woman with the issue touched only the hem of the Lord's garment. Men after a nighttime emission he leaves to their own conscience.

Gregory reached the opposite conclusion from the same Gospel story. If the woman with the issue could rightly touch the Lord's garment, he wrote to Augustine of Canterbury, a woman in her monthly period may enter church and receive communion, since what nature brings is no crime. A woman who holds back out of reverence is to be commended, and one who receives is not to be judged. Bede preserved the letter in his history of the English church.

16.overview:
After the death of Nadab and Abihu, the LORD tells Moses that Aaron may not enter the room behind the veil whenever he likes. Once a year he goes in wearing plain linen, carrying incense and the blood of a bull for himself and of a goat for the people, and sprinkles it on and before the mercy seat. A second goat, chosen by lot, has Israel's confessed sins laid on its head and is led away into the wilderness. The day is fixed as the tenth of the seventh month, a day of fasting and rest.

Watch what the blood cleanses. The high priest makes atonement for the holy place itself, “because of the uncleanness of the children of Israel” (v. 16), and v. 33 lists sanctuary, tent, altar, priests, and people. The day cleans God's house as well as his people, so that he can go on dwelling “in the midst of their uncleanness.”

16.hermeneutics:
Sending evil away on a live animal was an old practice. In the Hittite ritual of Ashella (CTH 394), when plague struck an army, its commanders decked rams with colored wool, laid their hands on them, drove them through the camp, and released them at the border of an enemy land; a decorated woman was sent the same way for the king. Two texts from Ebla in Syria (24th century BC) describe a she-goat with a silver bracelet driven into the wasteland of Alini as part of the purifications for a royal wedding. Leviticus keeps the live animal, the laid-on hands, and the trip out of bounds. What the goat carries differs. It bears Israel's iniquities, spoken aloud in confession (v. 21), and it goes to “a land not inhabited” (v. 22), every year rather than in an emergency.

Temples needed cleansing too. In the Babylonian New Year festival, known from Seleucid-era tablets, Nabu's shrine Ezida was purged on the fifth day: a ram was beheaded, its carcass rubbed against the shrine, and the exorcist and the slaughterer threw it into the river and stayed out of the city until the festival ended. Leviticus 16 is also about a building. The blood purges the holy place, the tent, and the altar (vv. 16, 18–19), and the men who lead the goat away and burn the carcasses must wash before they come back into the camp (vv. 26, 28). The difference is the source of the dirt. Here it is Israel's own uncleanness and sin, which have seeped into the sanctuary (v. 16).

notes: **Atonement:** the verb *kipper*, “make atonement,” occurs 16 times in the chapter. Five of them come in the closing vv. 32–34, which sum up everything the day atones for.
**Sevens:** blood is sprinkled seven times before the mercy seat (v. 14) and seven times on the altar (v. 19), inside and then outside.
**Two lots:** one goat is “for the LORD,” the other for *Azazel* (v. 8; KJV “scapegoat”). The word occurs four times (vv. 8, 10 twice, 26) and nowhere else in the Bible.
**Linen:** Aaron puts on plain linen to go in (v. 4) and leaves it in the tent when he comes out (v. 23), so the inner rite has its own garments.

Verse 1 reaches back over chs. 11–15 to the death of Nadab and Abihu, who came near the wrong way (10:1–2); ch. 16 tells how the high priest may come near and live. It also answers 15:31, which warns that Israel's uncleanness defiles the tabernacle. The rite stands between the purity laws (chs. 11–15) and the holiness laws (chs. 17–26).
**Later echoes:** Leviticus 23:27–32 sets the day among Israel's appointed times, and the jubilee is announced by trumpet “in the day of atonement” (25:9).

traditions.text: Amulek teaches that there must be a great and last sacrifice, not of beast or fowl but infinite and eternal, and that it will put a stop to the shedding of blood. He calls this “the whole meaning of the law,” every part of it pointing to the Son of God. Leviticus 16 is the law's yearly high point of blood and atonement, which is the system Amulek says that sacrifice fulfills.

Christ speaks as the advocate who pleads with the Father, asking him to behold the sufferings and death of one who did no sin and “the blood of thy Son which was shed.” On that basis he asks the Father to spare those who believe. In Leviticus the high priest carries blood into God's presence for the people; here the Son presents his own.

Abinadi explains that Israel was given a strict law of performances and ordinances, and that all of them were types of things to come. He then quotes Isaiah's suffering servant, who “shall bear their iniquities,” the same English words the KJV uses of the goat in v. 22.

The tractate on this chapter recalls the rite in the Second Temple. The high priest was moved to a chamber in the temple seven days beforehand, with a deputy ready in case he became unfit. At the scapegoat he confessed the people's sins and spoke God's name aloud, and priests and people in the court knelt and fell on their faces when they heard it.

traditions.source: Mishnah Yoma, on the crimson strip
traditions.text: Leviticus says only that the goat is let go in the wilderness. The Mishnah says a strip of crimson wool was tied to its head, then split between its horns and a rock, and the goat was pushed backward off a cliff. Rabbi Ishmael adds that a crimson strip at the sanctuary turned white when the goat reached the wilderness, reading Isaiah 1:18, “though your sins be as scarlet.”

Under Simeon the Just, the Talmud says, the lot “for the LORD” always came up in the high priest's right hand and the crimson strip turned white. For the forty years before the temple fell, the lot never came up in the right hand and the strip stayed red. The story treats v. 8's lots and the later crimson thread as signs of whether the day's atonement was accepted.

The tractate ends by limiting what the day can do. It atones for sins between a person and God, but not for wrongs against another person until that person is appeased; Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah draws this from “before the LORD” in v. 30. Whoever says “I will sin and the Day of Atonement will atone” gains no atonement.

Here Azazel is a fallen angel who taught humankind forbidden arts. The angel Raphael is told to bind him hand and foot and cast him into darkness in a desert place called Dudael, under rough and jagged rocks, until the judgment; “to him ascribe all sin.” The book reads the name in v. 8 as a person, which shapes the later debate over who or what Azazel is.

Josephus describes the day as a fast until evening. His details differ from Leviticus in places: the high priest sprinkles the blood seven times on the ceiling and on the floor, and the slain goat is burned with its skin “within the limits of the camp” in a clean place, where v. 27 says outside the camp.

Hebrews builds its account of Christ's work on this chapter. The high priest entered the second room once a year, “not without blood,” for himself and the people. Christ entered once into heaven itself with his own blood, not the blood of goats and calves, and does not need to repeat it as the high priest did every year.

Verse 27 sends the bodies of the bull and goat, whose blood went inside, to be burned outside the camp. Hebrews notes this rule and says Jesus likewise suffered outside the gate, then urges readers to “go forth therefore unto him without the camp.”

Barnabas reads the two goats as Christ. In its version the goats must be alike, the people spit on the cursed goat, and scarlet wool is wound on its head before it is driven out and the wool left in a thorn bush. When Christ returns in a scarlet robe, it says, people will recognize the one they crucified; its scarlet wool runs parallel to the Mishnah's crimson strip.

Arguing with a Jewish teacher, Justin says the two goats of the fast announced the two appearances of Christ. The goat sent away pictures his first coming, when the elders and priests rejected him; the other points to his second, when he will be recognized in Jerusalem.

17.overview:
Any ox, lamb, or goat an Israelite slaughters must be brought to the door of the tabernacle and offered there as a peace offering; a man who kills one anywhere else is charged with shedding blood. Every burnt offering and sacrifice, from Israelite or stranger, goes to the same door. No one may eat blood. A hunter who catches game must pour out its blood and cover it with dust, and anyone who eats an animal found dead or torn must wash.

The reason sits at the center, in v. 11: “the life of the flesh is in the blood.” Because blood is life, it has only two proper places. It goes on the altar, where God has given it “to make an atonement for your souls,” or into the ground under dust. It never goes into the mouth.

17.hermeneutics:
Across the ancient world, blood was food for spirits. In Homer's *Odyssey* (book 11), Odysseus digs a trench, cuts the throats of two sheep so the blood runs in, and the ghosts swarm up from below; the prophet Teiresias must drink before he can speak. Hurrian and Hittite rituals opened pits for the gods of the underworld, and the victim's blood was smeared on the rim or run down into the hole, as excavated pits at Urkesh in Syria bear out. Against that background the chapter's rules have an edge. Blood left open on the ground could feed whatever lived below. Leviticus sends it to the altar or covers it with dust (v. 13), and v. 7 names the alternative: sacrifices in the open field to “devils,” Hebrew *se'irim*, literally “goats,” the satyrs of Isaiah 13:21.

Israel also believed that uncovered blood cries out. Abel's blood cries to God from the ground (Genesis 4:10). Job pleads, “O earth, cover not thou my blood” (Job 16:18), so that his case stays open. Ezekiel charges Jerusalem with setting blood on a bare rock instead of covering it with dust, so that it calls for vengeance (Ezekiel 24:7–8). That explains the hard words of v. 4. A man who kills an ox away from the altar has not returned its life to God, and so “he hath shed blood,” the language used of killing a person.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, five short laws with the reason for them at v. 11.
notes: **Same opening:** laws 1–4 each begin with the doubled Hebrew *ish ish*, “whatsoever man” (vv. 3, 8, 10, 13). From v. 8 on, each also names “the strangers which sojourn among you.”
**Blood:** the word *dam* occurs 13 times in 16 verses, three times in v. 14 alone.
**Cut off:** the penalty “cut off” comes four times (vv. 4, 9, 10, 14), once in each of the first four laws. The fifth law, on carcasses, ends instead with bearing iniquity (v. 16).

Ch. 17 opens the last large block of the book, chs. 17–26, which scholars since 1877 call the Holiness Code after its refrain “ye shall be holy” (19:2; 20:7, 26). The block ends with the summary at 26:46. The chapter's subject, blood, ties it back to ch. 16, where blood cleanses the sanctuary.

**Later echoes:** Saul's hungry troops slaughter on the ground and eat “with the blood,” and Saul has a great stone rolled up to slaughter on (1 Samuel 14:32–34). Deuteronomy 12:15–24 allows slaughter far from the sanctuary but says to pour the blood out “as water.”

traditions.text: The JST expands the blood command given to Noah. The blood of all flesh given for meat is to be shed upon the ground and not eaten, blood is not to be shed except for meat to save life, and God will require the blood of every beast at man's hands. It gives the rule of Leviticus 17 a setting long before Sinai, as Jubilees also does.

The Lord says that beasts and fowls are ordained for man's food and clothing, so forbidding meat is not of God. The same passage adds a limit: a woe on the man who sheds blood “or that wasteth flesh and hath no need.” Like Leviticus 17, it treats the killing of an animal as something God takes account of, even when the meat is lawful to eat.

Amulek foresees that the great and last sacrifice will bring a stop to the shedding of blood and fulfill the law of Moses. After his resurrection, Christ's voice tells the Nephites to offer him no more the shedding of blood, but “a broken heart and a contrite spirit.” Verse 11 gives blood to Israel upon the altar to atone; these passages describe that use of blood ending.

Jubilees traces the blood law to Noah, who with his sons swore never to eat blood, and says it is written on the heavenly tablets with no limit of days. Moses is told to command Israel to eat no blood, so that the blood of their offerings may seek forgiveness for them before the altar. Verse 11's two ideas, no blood eaten and blood for atonement, are already joined here.

Summarizing the law for Greek readers, Josephus says Moses forbade blood as food altogether and “esteemed it to contain the soul and spirit.” He puts v. 11's “life” in the terms Greek readers would know, soul and spirit, and in the same breath forbids the flesh of an animal that died of itself, the case v. 15 treats, and the fat of goats, sheep, and bulls.

The rabbis worked out v. 13 as a standing duty. Covering the blood applies in the land of Israel and abroad, with or without a temple, to wild animals and birds but not to domestic cattle or to sacrifices. Because it does not depend on the altar, the rule outlived the temple, and observant Jews still cover the blood of slaughtered fowl and game with dust or earth.

On v. 7 Rashi, following the Sifra, takes *se'irim* as demons and points to the same word in Isaiah 13:21. On v. 11 he says the life of every creature, not only sacrificial animals, depends on its blood, so God set blood on the altar to atone for human life: “let life come and expiate for life.” On v. 13 he notes that the verb “hunteth” teaches a person to eat meat only after some toil in preparing it.

The Jerusalem council asks Gentile believers to abstain from things offered to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication. Many interpreters connect the list with Leviticus 17–18, the laws that bind “the stranger” as well as Israel. James had just noted that Moses is read in the synagogues every sabbath, and many readers take that as the reason for the list: shared tables with Jewish believers.

Hebrews says that under the law almost everything is cleansed with blood, and “without shedding of blood is no remission.” It is a summary of v. 11's principle, which Hebrews then applies to the blood of Christ.

Answering the charge that Christians drank human blood, Tertullian says they do not even have the blood of animals at their meals and avoid things strangled or dead of themselves. Persecutors, he says, tempted Christians with blood sausages, knowing they would refuse. Over a century after Acts 15, the blood rule was still a mark of Christian practice in North Africa.

traditions.source: Letter of the churches of Vienne and Lyons, in Eusebius
traditions.text: During the persecution at Lyons, a woman named Biblis, who had at first denied Christ, turned on her torturers. She asked how people who think it unlawful to taste even the blood of animals could eat children, then confessed herself a Christian. Her answer shows the same practice Tertullian describes in another province.

18.overview:
The LORD tells Israel not to live by the customs of Egypt, which they have left, or of Canaan, where they are going, but by his statutes, which a man is to keep and “live in them” (v. 5). A list follows of close relatives with whom sexual relations are forbidden: parents, stepmother, sisters, granddaughters, aunts, daughter-in-law, sister-in-law, and a woman together with her daughter or her sister. Other prohibitions come next: relations during menstruation, adultery, giving children to Molech, homosexual intercourse, and bestiality.

Watch the land. The closing verses picture it as a body that is made unclean by these acts and vomits out its people (vv. 25, 28). The nations before Israel were expelled that way, and Israel is warned it can be too. The laws are presented as the terms of living in the land.

18.hermeneutics:
Other law codes also banned some unions inside the family. The Laws of Hammurabi (18th century BC) exile a man who has relations with his daughter (§154), drown a man who takes his son's bride (§155), and burn a son and mother who come together after the father's death (§157). Leviticus covers a wider circle of relatives and gives one reason for all of them: each woman is the “nakedness” of a near kinsman, and so in effect his own flesh (vv. 6–17). It also leaves the penalties to ch. 20. Here the weight falls on God's name, “I am the LORD,” and on the land itself, which reacts to defilement (vv. 24–28).

Verse 21 sets Molech among the sexual laws. The Hebrew word for “seed” joins it to v. 20, which speaks of seed given to a neighbor's wife; v. 21 speaks of seed, children, given to Molech. Biblical texts place the practice at Topheth in the valley of Hinnom, where children were made to “pass through the fire” (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 32:35). In Phoenician colonies such as Carthage, cemeteries now called tophets held urns of burned infants and young animals, and Punic inscriptions use *mlk* as a term for a kind of offering. Since Otto Eissfeldt's study of 1935, scholars have debated whether Molech in Leviticus is a god's name or the name of a sacrifice. Either way, v. 21 counts it as profaning the name of Israel's God.

structure.summary: Inclusio: warnings against the customs of the nations open and close the list of laws (vv. 1–5, 24–30).

open.text: Not the doings of Egypt and Canaan; keep my statutes

close.text: Defile not yourselves; the land spues out the nations

notes: **Statutes:** the Hebrew word for “statutes” or “ordinances” (*chuqqot*) appears only in the frame, at vv. 3, 4, 5 and again at vv. 26, 30. The nations' statutes are set against God's.
**Nakedness:** the word *ervah* occurs 24 times, all in vv. 6–19, the kinship laws. After v. 19 the language turns to defilement: “defile” occurs eight times in vv. 20–30.
**Signature:** “I am the LORD” (or “the LORD your God”) comes six times, four of them in the opening vv. 2–6, then at v. 21 and in the last verse.

Chs. 18–20 form a unit. Ch. 18 and ch. 20 cover much the same forbidden acts, first as commands and then with penalties, and both end with the land spewing out its inhabitants (18:28; 20:22). Ch. 19, the call to be holy, stands between them.
**Looking back and ahead:** v. 5, “he shall live in them,” is repeated twice by Ezekiel (Ezekiel 20:11, 13). Molech returns with its penalty in 20:2–5.

traditions.text: Nephi asks his brothers whether the people Israel drove out of Canaan were righteous, and answers no: they had rejected God's word and were ripe in iniquity. He adds that “the Lord esteemeth all flesh in one,” so Israel was favored for righteousness, not ancestry. The account matches vv. 24–28, where the land expels the nations for their deeds and can expel Israel for the same.

Moroni records God's decree for the promised land of the Jaredites: whatever nation possesses it must serve God or be swept off when it is “ripened in iniquity.” Like Leviticus 18, it ties holding a land to the conduct of the people on it, and it warns later possessors, as Leviticus warns Israel, that the same decree applies to them.

Abraham describes his fathers turning to the sacrifice of the heathen, offering their children to idols. The priest of Pharaoh offered men, women, and children on an altar in Chaldea, including a child as a thank-offering. It is the kind of child sacrifice v. 21 forbids under the name of Molech.

Retelling the story of Dinah, Jubilees says a man who gives his daughter or sister to a Gentile is to be stoned, because “he has given of his seed to Moloch.” It reads v. 21's “seed” as children lost to Israel through intermarriage. This is the very rendering of v. 21 that the Mishnah later forbids translators to use in the synagogue.

Philo opens his treatment of these laws by contrasting other peoples. He says the Persian magistrates married even their mothers, that Egyptian law let men marry their sisters whether younger or older, and that Solon and the Spartan lawgiver each allowed half-sister marriages on one side of the family only. Moses, he says, forbade all of them.

In his summary of the law, Josephus says Moses abhorred a man lying with his mother “as one of the greatest crimes,” along with the father's wife, aunts, sisters, and sons' wives. He adds that Moses ordained death for such offenses, drawing the penalties of ch. 20 into this list.

The rabbinic commentary on Leviticus reads the doubled “any man” of v. 6 (Hebrew *ish ish*) as including Gentiles, who are bound by these laws as Israel is. It reads the plural “ye shall not approach” as binding women as well as men. Both readings widen a list addressed to Israelite men.

When the rabbis ask why saving a life overrides the Sabbath, Shmuel cites v. 5: a person shall do the commandments “and live by them,” and not die by them. Rava calls this the one proof that cannot be refuted. A verse about obeying the law became the basis for setting most laws aside to save life.

The Mishnah rules on how these laws were read and translated in the synagogue. A reader who softens the forbidden-relations passage is silenced, and so is a translator who renders v. 21 as a ban on fathering children with an Aramean woman. Both are told to give the text as it stands.

The Qumran sect extended v. 13. Since a man may not marry his mother's sister, it reasoned, the rule applies to women as well, so a woman may not marry her father's brother; in effect it barred uncle-niece marriage. The rabbis took the other side and permitted it.

Following the Sifra, Rashi says v. 3 singles out Egypt and Canaan because their customs were the most corrupt, and the district of Egypt where Israel lived worse than the rest. He takes “their ordinances” to mean social customs that had the force of law, giving theaters and racecourses as examples.

Paul quotes v. 5 twice: “The man that doeth them shall live in them.” In both places he uses it to describe the righteousness that comes from keeping the law, which he sets beside righteousness by faith. In Galatians it follows a curse on whoever does not continue in everything the law requires (Galatians 3:10).

John the Baptist tells Herod Antipas, “It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife,” applying v. 16 to Herod's marriage to Herodias; it costs John his life. Paul condemns a man in Corinth who has his father's wife, the case of v. 8, as something not even the Gentiles name.

19.overview:
The LORD tells the whole congregation, “Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy” (v. 2), then spells out what that means in a long run of short laws. They mix worship and daily life: honor mother and father, keep the sabbaths, eat peace offerings on time, leave the edges of the field for the poor, pay a hired man before nightfall, judge fairly, hate no brother, love your neighbor as yourself. Later come rules on mixed seed and cloth, young fruit trees, mourning rites, the elderly, the stranger, and honest weights.

Notice the refrain. Law after law, or cluster after cluster, ends with “I am the LORD” or “I am the LORD your God.” The same signature that stands under the sabbath stands under the reaper's corners, the worker's wages, and the merchant's scales, so holiness reaches into the field and the market as much as the sanctuary.

19.hermeneutics:
Ancient kings claimed to protect the weak. Hammurabi says the gods called him to rule “so that the strong should not harm the weak,” and his epilogue says he set up his laws to protect widows and orphans. His code also fixes the daily wage of a hired laborer by season (§273). In Leviticus the duty passes from the king to every household. The farmer himself leaves the corners of his field and the fallen grapes for the poor and the stranger (vv. 9–10). The employer pays the hired man before morning, not at a rate set by the palace but on a deadline set by God (v. 13). The judge must not favor the poor or the mighty (v. 15).

Mourning in Canaan could draw blood. In the Ugaritic Baal cycle (14th–13th century BC), when the god El hears that Baal is dead, he comes down from his throne, puts dust on his head, and gashes his cheeks, chin, and arms with a blade. Prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel cut themselves “after their manner” (1 Kings 18:28). Verses 27–28 forbid exactly these rites for Israel: cutting the corners of the hair and beard, and cuts in the flesh for the dead. Israel's God does not die, and his people are not to grieve in the manner of those whose god did.

Holiness toward neighbor: poor, workers, courts, love
Holiness in field, body, and worship
Holiness toward the aged, the stranger, the buyer

notes: **Signature:** after the heading in v. 2, “I am the LORD” or “I am the LORD your God” closes a law or group of laws 15 times (vv. 3, 4, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 25, 28, 30, 31, 32, 34, 36, 37).
**Two loves:** the verb “love” occurs twice, “love thy neighbour as thyself” (v. 18) and, of the stranger, “love him as thyself” (v. 34). The second extends the first beyond Israel.
**The stranger:** the word *ger* occurs four times (vv. 10, 33, 34 twice), and v. 34 gives the reason: “ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.”

Ch. 19 is the center of chs. 18–20, flanked by two chapters on forbidden acts. Its opening command, “ye shall be holy,” first given with the food laws (11:44–45), becomes the motto of chs. 17–26 and returns at 20:7 and 20:26.
**Later echoes:** Leviticus 23:22 repeats the corners and gleanings, and Ruth 2 shows the law at work when Ruth the Moabitess, a stranger, gleans in Boaz's field.

traditions.text: Given in Zion, Jackson County, Missouri, to Saints newly arrived there, this revelation repeats the two great commandments: love God with all thy heart, and “thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.” It follows the second at once with commands not to steal, commit adultery, or kill, the same pairing of love with specific laws found in vv. 11–18.

Alma taught his people that every man should love his neighbor as himself, so that there would be no contention among them. In D&C 38 the Lord twice tells the Saints to esteem a brother as oneself, and joins it with practicing virtue and holiness. Both take v. 18 as the rule for building a community.

At the temple in Bountiful the risen Christ cites the saying “thou shalt love thy neighbor and hate thine enemy,” of which only the first half is in Leviticus. He then commands love for enemies, blessing on those who curse, and prayer for persecutors, as in Matthew 5:43–44.

On v. 18 Rabbi Akiva calls love of neighbor an all-embracing principle of the Torah. Ben Azzai answers that Genesis 5:1, the book of the generations of Adam, states a greater principle still, which commentators explain as taking in every human being descended from Adam. The same passage reads the ban on revenge narrowly, as applying to the children of one's own people.

Rabbi Hiyya says this chapter was spoken to the whole assembly (v. 2) because most of the essentials of the Torah depend on it. Rabbi Levi adds that it contains the Ten Commandments, and pairs them verse by verse: “I am the LORD your God” with Exodus 20:2, molten gods with no other gods, false oaths with taking God's name in vain, sabbaths with the sabbath command, and revering mother and father with honoring them. On this reading ch. 19 restates Sinai for daily life.

A Gentile asks to be taught the whole Torah while standing on one foot. Shammai drives him off; Hillel tells him, “That which is hateful to you do not do to another,” and calls the rest commentary. The saying is widely read as Hillel's version of v. 18, stated in the negative.

Rashi defines the two sins of v. 18 with an example from the Sifra. If a neighbor refused to lend you his sickle and you refuse to lend him your hatchet, that is revenge. If you lend it but say you are not like him, that is bearing a grudge.

A whole tractate is built on v. 9. It opens by listing the corners of the field among the things with no fixed measure, then says not less than a sixtieth should be left, more depending on the field, the yield, and the number of poor. In that opening list the corners stand beside acts of kindness and the study of Torah, things a person can never do too much of.

Asked for the great commandment, Jesus joins Deuteronomy 6:5 to v. 18 and says all the law and the prophets hang on these two. In Luke the lawyer recites the two commands himself, Jesus tells him to do this and live, echoing Leviticus 18:5, and the lawyer asks the follow-up, “And who is my neighbour?”, and Jesus answers with the parable of the Samaritan, the kind of outsider v. 34 also commands Israel to love.

Paul says the commandments against adultery, killing, stealing, false witness, and coveting are summed up in v. 18, and that all the law is fulfilled in this one word. James calls it “the royal law.” Rabbi Akiva's later judgment in the Sifra runs on the same line.

Peter quotes the command, “Be ye holy; for I am holy,” which Leviticus gives at 11:44–45 and again in v. 2, and applies it to believers' whole way of life. The command addressed to Israel at Sinai becomes the call of scattered Christian communities in Asia Minor.

This early church manual opens with “the way of life”: first love the God who made you, second your neighbor as yourself. It adds the negative Golden Rule, close to Hillel's saying, and later tells readers to love some people more than their own life.

20.overview:
The LORD sets penalties for offenses already forbidden in ch. 18. Whoever gives a child to Molech is to be stoned, and if the people look away, God himself will cut off that man, his family, and all who follow him. Those who turn to mediums face the same. After a call to be holy, a list follows: cursing a parent, adultery, forbidden unions within the family, and lying with an animal. Most carry death; some carry being cut off or dying childless. The chapter closes by warning that the land will vomit Israel out as it did the nations, and orders the medium and wizard put to death.

Ch. 18 said what not to do; ch. 20 says what happens when it is done. The order also shifts. Molech, near the end of ch. 18 (18:21), now heads the list, and mediums frame the chapter at both ends (vv. 6, 27). Turning to other powers comes first.

20.hermeneutics:
Israel's neighbors also punished sexual offenses inside the family. The Code of Hammurabi burns a man and his mother together (§157), drowns a man who takes his son's bride (§155), and only banishes a man who lies with his daughter (§154). The Hittite Laws put to death a man who takes a woman and her daughter, or his brother's wife while the brother lives (§195), but excuse intercourse with a stepmother once the father is dead (§190). They also punish lying with a cow, pig, or dog by death, yet let a man go free after a horse or mule, though he may never become a priest (§§187, 199). Leviticus 20 covers much the same ground with fewer exceptions, and the reason it gives is not a wronged husband or father. The acts defile the land, and the land itself will vomit out those who do them (vv. 22–23).

Molech is tied to burning children in the valley of Hinnom (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 32:35). Greek writers say Carthage, a Phoenician colony, did the same: Diodorus Siculus reports that in 310 BC the city burned two hundred children of noble families to Kronos, laying them on the hands of a bronze statue above a fire pit (20.14). Excavated precincts at Carthage hold urns of burned infant bones, and Punic inscriptions use the word *mlk* for a kind of offering. Scholars still debate whether Molech was a god or a sacrifice. Leviticus treats him as a figure to “go a whoring after” (v. 5).

The word for one with a “familiar spirit” (*ob*, v. 27) has relatives in Hittite and Akkadian words for a ritual pit dug to call up the dead, which may be what the woman of Endor did when Saul asked her to “bring me him up” (1 Samuel 28:8).

open.text: Molech worship; turning to mediums and wizards

close.text: The medium and the wizard put to death

notes: **Penalties step down:** “Surely be put to death” (*mot yumat*) comes 9 times, all in vv. 2–16 and v. 27. Vv. 17–21 move to being cut off, bearing iniquity, and dying childless.
**Repetition to watch:** “Their blood shall be upon them” (or “him”) comes 6 times (vv. 9, 11, 12, 13, 16, 27). “Cut off” comes 5 times (vv. 3, 5, 6, 17, 18).
**Separation:** The verb for separate (*badal*) comes 4 times in vv. 24–26. God separated Israel from the peoples, so Israel separates clean animals from unclean.

Chs. 18–20 form one block on holiness in family and community. Ch. 18 opens with “ye shall not walk in their ordinances” (18:3) and ch. 20 closes the block with the same warning (20:23) and the same threat of a land that vomits out its people (18:28; 20:22). Ch. 21 turns from the people to the priests.
**Links:** V. 25 reaches back to the clean and unclean animals of ch. 11. The call “be ye holy” (v. 7) is quoted in 1 Peter 1:16.

traditions.text: The “law” given to the Church in Ohio keeps the command against adultery but sets a different penalty. One who commits adultery and does not repent “shall be cast out,” and one who repents with all his heart is to be forgiven. Cases are tried before two or more elders on the word of two witnesses, and the Church lifts hands against the guilty. Murder, by contrast, is handed over to the laws of the land.

Moroni records a decree about the land of promise that matches vv. 22–23. Whatever nation possesses this land of promise “shall serve God, or they shall be swept off,” and not until they are ripe in iniquity. Leviticus says the same of Canaan: the nations were cast out for their deeds, and Israel will be spued out if it does likewise.

The Mishnah's list of those to be stoned draws most of its entries from this chapter: the Molech worshiper, the medium and wizard, the one who curses a parent, and several forbidden unions. It narrows the Molech offense: a man is liable only if he both hands his child to Molech's priests and passes it through the fire. The medium is one from whose armpit the dead seem to speak.

The rabbinic commentary on Leviticus asks why the animal in vv. 15–16 must die: if the man sinned, what sin did the beast commit? Its answer is that the animal brought a man to ruin. It then argues from lesser to greater: if a beast is killed for that, how much more will God remove a person who leads another from life to death.

The Hebrew word behind “a wicked thing” in v. 17 is *chesed*, usually “kindness.” Sifra explains the oddity with Cain: if someone objects that Cain married his sister, the answer is that it was a kindness, for the world was first built by kindness (Psalm 89:2). Rashi repeats the reading and adds that the word means “disgrace” in Aramaic. Augustine faced the same question about Cain's generation (below).

On v. 26, “I have separated you from the peoples, to be mine,” Rabbi Elazar teaches that a person should not say he has no wish to eat pork. He should say that he would like to, but his Father in heaven has forbidden it. Keeping apart from sin, in this reading, is an act of accepting God's rule, not a matter of taste.

Summarizing the law of Moses for Greek readers, Josephus says Moses forbade adultery entirely and counted a man lying with his mother “as one of the greatest crimes.” He lists the other unions of chs. 18 and 20, from a father's wife to a son's wife, and says Moses ordained death for those who committed them.

Jesus quotes v. 9 (with Exodus 21:17), “Whoso curseth father or mother, let him die the death,” against the custom of declaring goods *Corban*, a gift to God, so that parents could not be helped by them. He takes the severity of the penalty as proof that God's command to honor parents outweighs the tradition.

John the Baptist is imprisoned for telling Herod Antipas, “It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife.” Herodias was the wife of Herod's living brother Philip. The union is the one v. 21 calls unclean; the exception for a brother who died childless (Deuteronomy 25:5) did not apply.

The scribes and Pharisees bring Jesus a woman taken in adultery and say Moses commanded “that such should be stoned.” V. 10 sets death for both the adulterer and the adulteress, though it names no method, and Deuteronomy 22:24 names stoning for a betrothed woman. No man is brought with her.

Peter tells Gentile believers to be holy in all their conduct, because it is written, “Be ye holy; for I am holy.” The command appears in Leviticus at 11:44, 19:2, and 20:7 and 26. Peter applies to a scattered church what Leviticus addressed to a people set apart from the nations.

Before the council Stephen quotes Amos 5:26 in its Greek form: Israel “took up the tabernacle of Moloch” in the wilderness. Leviticus forbids Molech worship to the generation at Sinai, and Stephen charges that the same generation carried his shrine anyway.

Augustine explains why the first generations married sisters, as necessity required, while later law condemned it. Spreading kinship across many households binds more people together in affection, while marrying a sister folds several relationships into one person. Like Sifra, he sets the law of v. 17 against Cain's marriage, but reasons from social bonds instead of divine kindness.

21.overview:
Moses gives the priests their own rules. A priest may not make himself unclean for the dead, except for his closest family. He may not shave his head, trim the edge of his beard, or cut his flesh in mourning, and he may not marry a harlot or a divorced woman. The high priest is held tighter still. He mourns no one, not even his father or mother, and must marry a virgin of his own people. Last, a son of Aaron with a blemish may not offer at the altar, though he still eats the holy bread.

The rules tighten in steps as one comes closer to the altar. Ch. 19 asks all Israel not to cut themselves for the dead (19:28). Ordinary priests also avoid most corpses, and the high priest avoids every one. The same line marks each of the three sections: “I the LORD” sanctify him, or them (vv. 8, 15, 23).

21.hermeneutics:
Babylonian diviners were screened by birth and body. A text tracing the diviner's craft back to Enmeduranki, a king of Sippar before the Flood, requires a candidate fathered by a priest “of pure descent,” and only “if he is without blemish in body and limbs” may he approach the gods Shamash and Adad, where the omens are read. Leviticus 21 has both requirements: a line of descent, “the seed of Aaron” (v. 21), guarded by marriage rules (vv. 7, 13–15), and a whole body for whoever approaches the altar (vv. 17–23). The difference is what the excluded man keeps. Aaron's son with a blemish loses the altar but not the table; he still eats “the bread of his God” (v. 22), the most holy portions included.

The mourning customs forbidden in v. 5 are attested at Ugarit in Syria. In the Baal myth (13th century BC), when the high god El hears that Baal is dead, he comes down from his throne to sit on the ground, pours dust on his head, and puts on sackcloth. Then he cuts his skin with a stone, gashes his cheeks and chin, and plows his chest “like a garden.” The goddess Anat mourns Baal the same way, and the prophets of Baal cut themselves at Carmel (1 Kings 18:28). Leviticus denies its priests the shaved head, the trimmed beard, and the cut skin, and denies the high priest even the uncovered head and torn clothes (v. 10). A corpse made anyone who touched it unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11), and the priest's work could not wait seven days.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence through three groups of priests, each section marked by the same refrain.
notes: **Refrain:** “I the LORD” who sanctifies (*meqaddesh*) marks each section (vv. 8, 15, 23). Ch. 22 carries the same line three more times.
**Repetition to watch:** the verb “profane” (*chalal*) comes 7 times (vv. 4, 6, 9 twice, 12, 15, 23). “The bread of” God comes 5 times (vv. 6, 8, 17, 21, 22).
**Blemish:** the word *mum* comes 5 times in vv. 17–23, framing a list of twelve defects in vv. 18–20.

Chs. 21–22 turn from the holiness of the people (chs. 18–20) to the holiness of those who handle holy things. The section opens with words to the priests (21:1) and ends with God hallowed among Israel (22:32–33). Ch. 23 then turns to holy times.
**Links:** Lev 10:6 had already forbidden Aaron's family to mourn Nadab and Abihu. Ezekiel 44:20–25 restates these rules for the temple of his vision.

traditions.text: The descent rules of this chapter still matter in Restoration scripture. The lesser priesthood bears Aaron's name because it “was conferred upon Aaron and his seed,” and a literal descendant of Aaron, if the firstborn, has a legal right to the bishopric. Such a descendant must still be designated by the First Presidency, found worthy, and ordained.

The revelation on priesthood promises that the sons of Moses and of Aaron will offer an acceptable offering in the Lord's house, to be built in that generation. It then widens the family: those faithful in obtaining the two priesthoods and magnifying their calling “become the sons of Moses and of Aaron.” Leviticus 21 limits the altar to Aaron's physical seed; D&C 84 opens the title to the faithful.

Josephus says Moses gave the priests “a double degree of purity.” He adds to the banned wives a slave, a captive, and a woman who kept an inn, and he lets an ordinary priest marry a widow but not the high priest. The high priest may not approach any corpse, while other priests may for near kin, and a blemished priest shares the priests' portion but may not go up to the altar. He also forbids priests wine while they wear the sacred garments, a rule Leviticus gives in 10:9.

Philo lists what the law asks of a priest's body: whole, with nothing missing or added, and skin free of scab and sores. He reads these demands as “symbols of the purity of his soul.” If the body that serves must be inspected so closely, he argues, the soul made in the image of God must be inspected far more. Hebrews makes a similar move from body to character (below).

V. 1 says “Speak” and then “say unto them,” and Rashi, following the Talmud, takes the doubling as a charge to the adult priests to keep their children from corpses too. V. 2 lists the near kin a priest may mourn but leaves out a wife, so Rashi, following Sifra, reads “his kin, that is near unto him” as meaning his wife.

traditions.text: The Mishnah pictures the high priest at a family funeral under v. 11. He may not follow the bier. As the mourners turn down one street out of sight, he steps into the street they left, and so he walks behind them at a distance as far as the city gate. The same passage says he may not marry his brother's widow, since v. 14 bars any widow.

In the Chamber of Hewn Stone the great Sanhedrin examined each priest's descent and body. One found unfit put on black and left; one found fit put on white and went in to serve. When no blemish was found in Aaron's seed they held a feast and blessed God, who chose Aaron and his sons.

The Mishnah works out what v. 23 leaves a blemished priest to do. In a corner chamber of the women's court, priests with defects sorted the altar wood and threw out any piece with worms. The tractate Bekhorot rules that every blemish that disqualifies an animal (22:22–24) also disqualifies a priest, and then adds defects found only in people, such as the shape of the head.

The Mishnah ranks priest above Levite and Levite above Israelite, much as this chapter guards the priest's line. Then it adds a limit. A person of the most flawed descent who is learned in the Torah comes before a high priest who is ignorant. Birth sets the order only among equals in wisdom.

Hebrews describes Jesus in the language of this chapter: a high priest “holy, harmless, undefiled, separate from sinners.” It sets him against the high priests made by the law, who “have infirmity” and must offer first for their own sins. The flawless body asked of Aaron's sons becomes, in Hebrews, a sinless life.

Tertullian cites Leviticus as saying that God's priests must not marry more than once, apparently reading the high priest's marriage rule (vv. 13–14). He then asks, “Are not even we laics priests?” and quotes Revelation 1:6. If every Christian is a priest, he argues, the rule binds the laity too, especially since clergy are chosen from among them.

22.overview:
A priest who is unclean, from a skin disease, a discharge, a corpse, or a creeping thing, must keep away from the holy food until he has washed and the sun has set. Only the priest's household may eat it: his bought slaves and those born in his house, and a daughter widowed or divorced without children who comes home, but not a guest, a hired worker, or a daughter married outside the priesthood. Anyone who eats it by mistake repays it with a fifth added. Animals offered must be without blemish, and a newborn stays with its mother seven days. Mother and young may not be killed on the same day.

The animal on the altar is held to nearly the same test as the priest who offers it. The blemish list in v. 22 repeats words from 21:18–20: blind, broken, scurvy, scabbed, and, a verse later, “superfluous.” Priest and offering both come to the altar whole.
