22.hermeneutics:
A Hittite text of about 1400 BC, the Instructions for Priests and Temple Personnel, sets rules for the staff who prepare the gods' meals. The kitchen must be swept, no pig or dog may cross its threshold, and the cooks and bakers must bathe, wear clean clothes, and trim their hair and nails. A man who has slept with a woman must bathe before the gods' morning meal. One who comes near the gods' bread unclean, and a colleague who covers for him, both die. Vv. 3–7 share the concerns: a man “whose seed goeth from him” or who touches something unclean washes, waits for sunset, and only then eats; one who comes near unclean is cut off “from my presence.” In Leviticus, though, the priest eats the holy food himself, “because it is his food” (v. 7).

The same instructions forbid staff to carry the gods' bread home to their wives, sons, or servants, and a stranger not of the Hittite capital who approaches the gods is to die. Leviticus draws the line around the priest's house instead. Slaves he bought and those born in his house eat, and so does a daughter who returns home childless, but a guest or a hired worker may not (vv. 10–13).

The Hittite staff are also warned against keeping a fattened ox or sheep for themselves and handing the god a haggard one, thinking a god will say nothing. Malachi 1:8 makes the same charge in Israel: would the governor accept the blind and lame? Vv. 20–25 rule such animals out in advance.

notes: **Refrain:** “I am the LORD” comes 9 times (vv. 2, 3, 8, 9, 16, 30, 31, 32, 33). Three of them read “I the LORD” who sanctifies (vv. 9, 16, 32), which brings that line to seven uses since 20:8.
**Shared list:** Five defects in vv. 22–23 use the same Hebrew roots as the priest's list in 21:18–20 (blind, broken, scurvy, scabbed, superfluous).
**Holy things:** The noun *qodesh* (“holiness,” “holy thing”) comes 14 times, 13 of them in vv. 2–16.

Ch. 22 completes the section on priests and offerings that began at 21:1. Its last verses (vv. 31–33) gather the section's refrains: keep my commandments, do not profane my holy name, I am the LORD who hallows you and brought you out of Egypt. Ch. 23 turns to holy times.
**Links:** Malachi 1:6–14 accuses the priests of his day of breaking exactly these rules. 1 Peter 1:19 calls Christ “a lamb without blemish and without spot.”

traditions.text: Adam is commanded to offer the firstlings of his flocks, and he obeys without knowing why. After many days an angel asks him the reason and then supplies it: the offering is “a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten.” Read with that key, the unblemished male of v. 19 pictures the one who would be offered.

Amulek, teaching the Zoramites, says a great and last sacrifice must come, and it will be neither a man nor a beast nor a fowl but infinite and eternal. Then the shedding of blood will stop and the law of Moses will be fulfilled. The whole meaning of the law, he says, is “every whit pointing to that great and last sacrifice,” the Son of God.

After the destruction at his death, the voice of Christ tells the Nephites that their sacrifices and burnt offerings are done away and he will accept none of them. In place of the flawless animal of vv. 19–21, he asks for “a broken heart and a contrite spirit.”

Philo cites the law that keeps a newborn animal with its mother for its first seven days of nursing, and the ban on sacrificing mother and young on one day. To kill both together he calls “the greatest extravagance of barbarity.” He reads the laws as training in kindness, since mercy shown to animals teaches mercy to people.

On v. 27 the midrash reads Ecclesiastes 3:15 (KJV “God requireth that which is past”) as God seeking the pursued. Abel, Noah, Abraham, Joseph, Moses, David, and Israel were all pursued, and God chose them. So with offerings: the ox is hunted by the lion, the goat by the leopard, the lamb by the wolf, and God takes from the hunted, not the hunters.

This Aramaic paraphrase turns v. 28 into a call to imitate God. Israel is to be merciful on earth as their Father in heaven is merciful, and so neither cow nor ewe is to be slain with her young. The wording is close to Jesus' “Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.”

The rabbis did not limit v. 28 to the altar. The ban on killing an animal and its young on the same day, the Mishnah rules, applies in the land of Israel and outside it, while the temple stands and after it is gone, and to ordinary meat as well as sacrifices.

Not every sage liked turning these animal laws into lessons about God's mercy. The Mishnah silences a prayer leader who says, in effect, that God's mercy reaches even the bird's nest (Deuteronomy 22:6–7, the twin of v. 28). One explanation in the Talmud: he makes the commands of God into mercy when they are simply decrees of the King. The Targum and Philo read the same laws the other way.

“I will be hallowed among the children of Israel” (v. 32) became the source text for *kiddush ha-Shem*, sanctifying God's name by dying rather than sinning. The sages at Lod ruled that a person may break any command to save his life except idolatry, forbidden unions, and murder. Because the verse says God is hallowed among Israel, a public act means one before ten Jews. Rashi adds that a martyr must not count on a miracle.
traditions.cite: Sifra, Emor 9:5; Sanhedrin 74a; Rashi on Leviticus 22:32

traditions.text: Peter tells believers they were redeemed not with silver and gold but with the precious blood of Christ, “as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” The standard of vv. 19–21 for an acceptable offering becomes a description of Christ himself. Peter draws the same contrast between corruptible silver and costly blood that Hebrews draws between animal blood and Christ's.

Hebrews contrasts the blood of animals with the blood of Christ, “who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God.” In Leviticus the priest and the victim are separate, each checked for blemishes (chs. 21–22); in Hebrews the offerer and the offering are one.

Clement follows Philo closely. The law keeps the young with its mother the first seven days and forbids slaying mother and offspring together, he says, so that kindness to animals may check cruelty to people. He turns the point against the Greeks, who mocked the law while they exposed their own infants.

23.overview:
The LORD lists his appointed feasts, the days Israel is to proclaim as holy convocations. The weekly sabbath comes first. In the first month come Passover on the fourteenth day and seven days of unleavened bread. When Israel reaps in the land, a sheaf of the first grain is waved before the LORD, and fifty days are counted to a second offering of two leavened loaves. In the seventh month come a day of trumpets on the first day, the Day of Atonement on the tenth, and seven days of tabernacles from the fifteenth, with an eighth day added. A closing section tells Israel to take branches, rejoice, and live in booths, remembering the wilderness.

The year is built on the sabbath's number. A seventh day, seven days of unleavened bread, seven weeks to the loaves, a seventh month, and seven days in booths. The weekly rest is stretched across the whole calendar.

23.hermeneutics:
A small limestone tablet from Gezer, from about the 10th century BC, lists the farmer's year month by month: two months of ingathering, two of sowing, two of late sowing, a month of hoeing flax, a month of barley harvest, a month of harvest and measuring (or feasting), two months of vine tending, and a month of summer fruit. Leviticus 23 hangs its feasts on the same cycle. The sheaf of v. 10 is the first barley, cut in the season of Passover. The two loaves of v. 17 come seven weeks later, when the wheat is in (Exodus 34:22 calls it “the firstfruits of wheat harvest”). Tabernacles falls “when ye have gathered in the fruit of the land” (v. 39), at the ingathering that opens the Gezer list. A first hearer would know where in the farm year each feast fell without being told the month.

Neighboring temples also claimed the first of the crop. Hittite instructions for temple staff (about 1400 BC) list a monthly festival, a yearly festival, an autumn festival, and a spring festival among many others, and they tell farmers who bring bread or young animals to the gods to bring them on time, before any person eats. V. 14 makes the same rule for Israel: no bread, parched grain, or fresh ears until the day the sheaf is offered. The gods in the Hittite texts are fed by the offerings. In Leviticus the first sheaf is waved “to be accepted for you” (v. 11), and the rest of the harvest is then free to eat.

notes: **Five speeches:** “The LORD spake unto Moses” opens vv. 1, 9, 23, 26, and 33, dividing the chapter into sabbath and Passover, the harvest feasts, trumpets, atonement, and tabernacles.

**Repetition to watch:** “Holy convocation” (*miqra qodesh*) comes 11 times. “No servile work” comes 6 times, but the sabbath and the Day of Atonement forbid all work (vv. 3, 28, 30, 31). “A statute for ever” comes 4 times (vv. 14, 21, 31, 41).
**The gleaning law** (v. 22) repeats 19:9 in the middle of the harvest feasts, so the poor and the stranger are counted in the calendar.

Chs. 23–24 deal with holy time and its upkeep. Ch. 23 gives the yearly feasts; ch. 24 adds the lamp kept burning “continually” and the bread set out “every sabbath” (24:3, 8), then the case of the blasphemer. Ch. 25 extends the sabbath pattern to years.
**Forward links:** Numbers 28–29 sets the offerings for each feast. The New Testament places the gift of the Spirit at Pentecost (Acts 2:1) and Jesus' “living water” at Tabernacles (John 7:37–38).

traditions.text: The revelation on the Lord's day carries the language of v. 3 and v. 27 into the Restoration. It is “a day appointed unto you to rest from your labors” and to offer oblations and sacraments to the Most High. Food is to be prepared with singleness of heart, so that fasting may be perfect, which the revelation calls joy that is full.

Elijah appeared in the Kirtland Temple to fulfill Malachi's promise and committed the keys of turning the hearts of fathers and children. By the Jewish calendar that Sunday fell in the week of Passover, when Jewish families poured a cup for Elijah and hoped for his return; a 1977 Church magazine article points out the connection. The Passover of v. 5 became the occasion Jews most associated with Elijah's coming.

“The morrow after the sabbath” (v. 11) divided Jewish groups. The Pharisees read “sabbath” as the first day of Passover, so the sheaf was cut on the night after it; the Boethusians read it as Saturday. The Mishnah describes the reaping with great fanfare, the reaper asking the crowd three times about the sunset, the sickle, and the basket, to publicize the date against the Boethusians.

Josephus, a priest, sides with the Mishnah's reckoning. The sheaf of barley is offered on the second day of unleavened bread, the sixteenth of the month, and only then do the people eat from the new harvest. Fifty days later comes the feast the Hebrews call *Asartha*, with a loaf of leavened wheat bread.

The Mishnah ties each feast to a judgment. At Passover the world is judged for grain, at Pentecost for fruit of trees, on the New Year all people pass before God like sheep, and at Tabernacles the world is judged for water, meaning the coming year's rain. The first day of the seventh month (v. 24), a memorial of trumpets in Leviticus, became Rosh Hashanah, the New Year.

V. 27 commands Israel to “afflict your souls” but does not say how. The Mishnah defines it as five abstentions: no eating or drinking, no bathing, no anointing with oil, no wearing shoes, and no marital relations. A king and a new bride may wash their faces, according to the first opinion.

In the Second Temple, Tabernacles included a water ceremony not found in Leviticus. Each morning a golden jug was filled at the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar, and at night the Water-Drawing celebration lit every courtyard in Jerusalem. “Whoever has not seen” it, says the Mishnah, has never seen joy. This is the setting of John 7 (below).

The midrash reads the four kinds of v. 40 as four kinds of Israelites. The citron has taste and scent, like those with both Torah and good deeds; the palm has taste but no scent, the myrtle scent but no taste, the willow neither. God does not discard the willow; he binds all four in one bundle so that each atones for the others.

Paul reads the spring feasts as Christ's. Christ is the passover lamb sacrificed for us, so believers are to purge out old leaven and keep the feast with unleavened bread of sincerity. Risen from the dead, Christ is “the firstfruits of them that slept,” the sheaf of v. 10 that promises the harvest to follow.

The Spirit falls on the disciples “when the day of Pentecost was fully come.” Pentecost is the Greek name for the fiftieth day of vv. 15–16, a pilgrim feast that explains why Jews from many nations were in Jerusalem to hear Peter.

At the Feast of Tabernacles, “in the last day, that great day of the feast,” Jesus stands and calls the thirsty to come to him and drink. Spoken at the feast of the Siloam water ceremony (above), the offer of rivers of living water would have struck its hearers in that setting. John explains that he spoke of the Spirit.

In the late 2nd century the churches of Asia kept Easter on “the fourteenth day of the moon,” the day of v. 5 when Jews sacrificed the lamb, whatever weekday it fell on. Their bishop Polycrates claimed the custom from John and Philip. Victor of Rome tried to cut them off, and other bishops rebuked him.

In his *Banquet of the Ten Virgins* the speaker Tusiane reads vv. 39–43 as prophecy. The seventh month is the seventh millennium, the booth is the human body, and the feast will be kept when the body rises. The boughs become virtues: faith, study of scripture, charity, righteousness, and chastity. Leviticus Rabbah reads the same branches as kinds of people.
traditions.cite: Banquet of the Ten Virgins, Discourse 9.1–4

traditions.text: In his *Table Talk* a guest argues that the Jews worship Dionysus. He describes their autumn feast at the vintage, with tables of fruit set under “tabernacles made of vines and ivy,” a day of carrying palm branches and wands into the temple, and little trumpets like those of Greek Bacchic rites. He has the details of vv. 34–43 roughly right and their meaning wrong.

24.overview:
Two short laws for the sanctuary open the chapter. Israel is to bring pure beaten olive oil so the lamps on the golden lampstand burn every night, and twelve loaves are to be set in two rows on the golden table each Sabbath, with frankincense as their memorial; the priests eat them. Then comes a story. The son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father fights in the camp and curses, blaspheming the Name. He is held until the LORD rules: he must be stoned outside the camp. Laws on killing and injury follow, and the chapter closes with the sentence carried out.

The case laws sit inside the story, between the ruling and the stoning. Read in that frame, “eye for eye” helps answer a question no law had yet covered: does Israel's law bind a man whose father was a foreigner? Verse 22 answers it with one law for stranger and native.

24.hermeneutics:
Mesopotamian temples fed their gods. Each day meals of bread, beer, meat and fruit were set on a table before the divine statue, and the food then went to the temple staff. The twelve loaves of vv. 5–9 look like that kind of table, and the differences stand out. The bread is changed once a week, not served at mealtimes. Only the frankincense goes up in fire as the “memorial” (v. 7); the loaves themselves go to Aaron and his sons as most holy (v. 9). Twelve loaves, the number of the tribes, “taken from the children of Israel by an everlasting covenant” (v. 8), make the table a standing pledge of the covenant more than a meal for God.

The Laws of Hammurabi (Babylon, c. 1750 BC) also demand eye for eye and bone for bone (§§196–197), but they scale the penalty by rank. Injuring a freed man costs a fixed payment, and injuring a slave costs half his value (§§198–199). They can also punish by substitution: if a badly built house collapses and kills the owner's son, the builder's son is put to death (§230). Leviticus 24 binds the penalty to the person who did the harm, “so shall it be done to him” (v. 19), and applies it to the stranger as to the native (v. 22).

notes: **The center:** The ladder turns on the talion formula, where *tachat* (“for”) joins three pairs in v. 20. The laws mirror each other around it: man, beast, injury, then injury, beast, man.
**Continually:** *Tamid* occurs 4 times in vv. 1–9 (vv. 2, 3, 4, 8), three times for the lamp and once for the bread. The sanctuary half is about what never stops.
**Curse words:** The verb for blaspheming the Name comes 3 times (vv. 11, 16 twice) and the verb “curse” 4 times (vv. 11, 14, 15, 23), framing the story from the offense to the stoning.

The outline joins chs. 23–24. The feasts end with Moses declaring “the feasts of the LORD” (23:44), and ch. 24 opens a fresh speech (v. 1) on the lamp and bread, the sanctuary's nightly and weekly rhythm. The story of vv. 10–23 is the only narrative in Leviticus outside chs. 8–10. Chapter 25 begins a new speech set “in mount Sinai” (25:1).
**Later echo:** Naboth is falsely charged with blaspheming “God and the king,” carried out of his city, and stoned (1 Kings 21:10–13), the procedure of this chapter turned into a weapon.

traditions.text: At the temple in Bountiful the risen Jesus repeats the old rule, “an eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth,” and answers it with the command not to resist evil and to turn the other cheek. The words match the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:38–39). The rule he quotes stands in Exodus 21, Deuteronomy 19 and here in v. 20, where it belongs to a ruling that covers the stranger too.

The minutes that organized the first high council at Kirtland provide for a case the written word does not settle: the president “may inquire and obtain the mind of the Lord by revelation.” The Church's footnote to v. 12, where the blasphemer is held under guard until the LORD's will is shown, points to this verse. Moses' wait for a ruling becomes the pattern for a council facing a new question.

Philo counts the blasphemer as the first of four cases in which Moses asks and God answers. He calls the man the child of unequal parents who took after his Egyptian father, admiring a people who make a god of the earth and the Nile. Moses wanted to kill him on the spot, Philo says, but feared any punishment he could devise would be too light, so he chained him and prayed for a ruling. Stoning suited, Philo suggests, a man with a heart of stone.

Rashi gathers the rabbinic answers to where the man “went out” from (v. 10). In one, he had pitched his tent with Dan, his mother's tribe, was told that each man camps by his father's house (Numbers 2:2), lost the case in Moses' court, and came out cursing. In another, his father was the Egyptian whom Moses killed (Exodus 2:11–12). His mother's names are read as “peace” and “speech,” for a woman who greeted and chatted with every man.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Leviticus 24:10–11 (citing Sifra, Emor; Leviticus Rabbah 32:3–5)

traditions.text: In his summary of Moses' laws Josephus puts it bluntly: the blasphemer is stoned, hung on a tree all that day, and buried without honor (compare Deuteronomy 21:22–23). Describing the tabernacle, he says the loaves were unleavened, set in two piles of six with two vials of frankincense, and changed on the Sabbath. He reads the twelve loaves as the twelve months of the year, tying the table to time where later readers tied it to the tribes.

The Mishnah narrows the crime: a blasphemer is liable only if he pronounces the divine Name itself and curses it, and Rashi reads “blasphemed” in v. 11 the same way. During the trial the witnesses use a stand-in name, Yosei, which like the divine Name has four Hebrew letters. At the end the eldest witness repeats the exact words in a cleared court, and the judges stand and tear their garments, never to sew them fully again. Compare the high priest who “rent his clothes” at Jesus' trial (Matthew 26:65).

The rabbis tell of a standing miracle at the table of v. 6. At the pilgrim feasts the priests lifted the table to show the crowds the bread, which was as fresh when removed as when set out a week before; they find this in 1 Samuel 21:6, which speaks of “hot bread in the day when it was taken away.” A midrash in Rashi turns the same question into the blasphemer's sneer: a king eats fresh bread daily, not loaves nine days old.
traditions.cite: Chagigah 26b; Rashi on Leviticus 24:10 (citing Midrash Tanchuma)

traditions.text: When Pharisees object to the disciples plucking grain on the Sabbath, Jesus reminds them that David ate the shewbread, “which was not lawful for him to eat,” but only for the priests. The rule behind his words is v. 9, which gives the loaves to Aaron and his sons. Irenaeus builds on the story (below).

Irenaeus argues that David could eat the priests' bread because God had made him a priest, and “all the righteous possess the sacerdotal rank.” The Lord's apostles too are priests, he adds, who inherit neither lands nor houses but serve God and the altar continually. So the disciples, as priests, were free to eat.

Stephen is charged before the council with speaking “blasphemous words against Moses, and against God.” After his speech he is cast out of the city and stoned, and the witnesses lay their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul. The scene follows the outline of vv. 14 and 23: the offender taken outside, the witnesses first, the community stoning.

25.overview:
Speaking “in mount Sinai,” the LORD gives the land a Sabbath of its own. Every seventh year Israel neither sows nor prunes, and servants, strangers and animals all eat what grows by itself. After seven of these sevens a trumpet sounds on the Day of Atonement and the fiftieth year is hallowed as a jubilee: land goes back to its family, and Israelites sold into service go home. The rest of the chapter works out the details: fields, town houses, Levite property, loans, and Israelites sold into service.

The reason sits in v. 23: “the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me.” A sale of land is really a sale of harvests until the jubilee, priced by the years left. Verse 55 applies the same logic to people. Israelites belong to the LORD who brought them out of Egypt, so no one can own them for good.

25.hermeneutics:
Old Babylonian kings issued edicts of *mīšarum*, “equity,” that cancelled certain debts and freed people sold or pledged for debt, usually early in a reign. The best preserved, from Ammi-saduqa of Babylon (c. 1646 BC), voids loans of need while leaving business loans in force, and releases free citizens bound for debt but not slaves born into slavery. Such a release was called *andurārum*, the Akkadian cognate of *deror*, the “liberty” proclaimed in v. 10. Leviticus draws the same line between the Israelite who must go free and the bought foreign slave who need not (vv. 39–46). What it changes is the timing. Release no longer waits on a king's decree; it comes on a fixed calendar, so every buyer knows the date in advance and pays only for the years left (vv. 15–16).

Mesopotamian families sold land when they fell into debt, and some laws let them win it back. The Laws of Eshnunna (c. 1800 BC) give a man forced by poverty to sell his house the right to redeem it when the buyer sells it on (§39). Leviticus builds such rights into a ladder. The nearest kinsman redeems first (v. 25), then the seller himself if he recovers (vv. 26–27), and if neither can, the jubilee returns the field anyway (v. 28). Houses in walled cities, the kind of urban property most often traded, keep only a year's right of redemption (vv. 29–30), while village houses count as fields. The jubilee makes permanent loss of family land impossible on paper, whatever happened in practice.

notes: **Four steps down:** “If thy brother be waxen poor” opens each case (vv. 25, 35, 39, 47; the verb *mukh* 4 times). Each step is worse than the last, and each has its remedy: redemption, an interest-free loan, release at the jubilee, redemption by kin.
**Counted words:** *Yovel* (“jubilee”) occurs 14 times in the chapter, from v. 10 on. Words for redeeming come 19 times: the verb 10 times and the noun *ge'ullah* 9 times.
**The refrain:** The LORD “brought you forth” out of Egypt closes the loan law (v. 38), the servant law (v. 42) and the chapter (v. 55).

A new heading set “in mount Sinai” (v. 1) is matched by the closing line of 26:46, so chs. 25–26 form one speech: the law of the land, then the blessings and curses that hang on it. The curses return to this chapter's theme, with the land enjoying its sabbaths while Israel is in exile (26:34–35).

**Later echoes:** The kinsman's right of redemption is at work in Ruth 4:4 and Jeremiah 32:7–8. Ezekiel 46:17 speaks of “the year of liberty,” and Zedekiah's covenant to proclaim liberty, quickly broken, draws Jeremiah's rebuke (Jeremiah 34:8–17). The words of v. 10 were cast on Philadelphia's Liberty Bell in 1753.

traditions.text: Reorganizing the United Firm, the Lord says he built the earth and “all things therein are mine,” and that he will provide for the poor by making the rich low. Because the properties are his, those who hold them are stewards (vv. 55–56). Leviticus grounds the jubilee in the same claim, that the land belongs to the LORD and Israel holds it as his tenants (v. 23).

In Joseph F. Smith's vision of the dead, the Son of God appears in the spirit world “declaring liberty to the captives,” and messengers go out to proclaim liberty to those who were bound. Isaiah is seen among the righteous, honored for prophesying that the Redeemer would proclaim liberty (Isaiah 61:1). Isaiah's Hebrew word there is *deror*, the jubilee word of v. 10, the same passage Jesus reads at Nazareth (below).

Rashi asks the question every reader of v. 1 meets: what does the Sabbath year have to do with Mount Sinai, when every law was given there? Quoting the Sifra, he answers that the general rules and the fine details of this law were both given at Sinai, and so were those of every other commandment. The chapter becomes the proof text for the rabbinic claim that the whole law, down to its details, came from Sinai.

A scroll from Qumran Cave 11 reads v. 13, “ye shall return every man unto his possession,” together with Deuteronomy 15:2 and Isaiah 61:1, as a prophecy of the last days. Melchizedek, at the head of God's angels, proclaims liberty to the captives and forgives their sins, and the Day of Atonement falls at the end of the tenth jubilee. The scroll joins the jubilee, the trumpet on the Day of Atonement (v. 9), and Melchizedek in one picture.

Philo says the fiftieth year restores alienated land so that the tribal portions survive and no family is stripped of its lot. The law, he argues, protects both sides: it tells the buyer not to pay as for an everlasting possession but for a fixed number of years, and invites the seller or his kin to buy the land back. Fields consecrated by a vow are the exception, since what is given to God never becomes common again (compare 27:20–21).

Josephus says the name jubilee “denotes Liberty,” and that in that year debtors are freed and slaves set at liberty. He adds a procedure Leviticus does not give: seller and buyer meet and weigh the harvests taken against the money spent on the land. If the harvests are worth more, the seller simply takes the land back; if the expenses are greater, he pays the difference.

The rabbis read “all the inhabitants thereof” in v. 10 strictly: the jubilee applies only when all Israel lives on its land. So when Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh were carried into exile, the counting of jubilees ceased. The Talmud then wrestles with Jeremiah 34, where Jerusalem frees and re-enslaves its servants long after that exile.

In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus reads from Isaiah 61, the anointed one sent to set the bruised at liberty and to preach “the acceptable year of the Lord,” then declares the scripture fulfilled that day. Isaiah's year of release borrows the jubilee's word for liberty (v. 10). 11QMelchizedek (above) had read the same passage as a promise of the last days.

Clement cites the Sabbath year and the jubilee as proof that the law of Moses is humane. It leaves the land fallow so that the poor may eat what grows unaided, and in the fiftieth year restores each man's land, setting bounds to the desires of those who covet possessions. He adds that the law forbids taking interest from a brother (vv. 35–37), and he counts as a “brother” not only a blood relative but anyone of the same race and mind who shares the same word.

In a hostile sketch of Jewish origins, the Roman historian says the Jews first rested on the seventh day because it ended their toils, and later, won over by the pleasures of idleness, gave the seventh year to rest as well. Josephus records the other side of the same practice: Julius Caesar's decree excused Judea from tribute in the Sabbath year, when they neither plough nor gather fruit, and Herod's siege of Jerusalem in 37 BC met famine because it fell in such a year. Outsiders noticed the fallow year of vv. 2–7 because Jews kept it.

26.overview:
After two summary commands, no idols and keep the sabbaths, the LORD sets two futures before Israel. If they walk in his statutes, rain comes in season, harvest runs into vintage, enemies flee, and the LORD sets his tabernacle among them and walks among them as their God. If they refuse, punishment comes in rounds, each “seven times” worse: disease and defeat, a sky like iron, wild beasts, sword and plague and famine, and at last ruined cities, a desolate land, and exile. Yet even in exile, if they confess, the LORD will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham and will not cast them away.

Watch how people walk. The blessings end with the LORD walking among his people (v. 12). The curses turn on a different walk: Israel walks “contrary” to the LORD, and he walks contrary to them. The Hebrew word, *qeri*, occurs seven times here and nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible.

26.hermeneutics:
Mesopotamian law collections closed with blessings and curses. The epilogue of Hammurabi's laws (Babylon, c. 1750 BC) asks Shamash to lengthen the reign of any later king who keeps the king's words, and calls on the gods to curse one who changes them: Adad is to withhold rain and ruin his land by famine, and Bel to scatter his subjects. Leviticus 26 stands in the same place at the end of its laws, with the same kinds of threat, rain withheld and a people scattered. But here the threats fall on the whole people, not on a future king, and no list of gods is invoked; the LORD who gave the law speaks the sanctions himself.

The closest wording comes from treaties. In the succession treaty Esarhaddon of Assyria imposed on his vassals in 672 BC, the curses ask the gods to make the vassal's ground like iron so that nothing sprouts, and to keep rain from falling as it cannot fall from a sky of bronze. Elsewhere the treaty threatens that in hunger they will eat the flesh of their sons. Verse 19 makes “your heaven as iron, and your earth as brass,” Deuteronomy 28:23 has the metals the other way round, and v. 29 has the same famine curse. Read against such treaties, the chapter casts Israel as a vassal bound to a great king, the one who broke the yoke of Egypt (v. 13). The difference is the ending. Esarhaddon's curses stop at ruin, while Leviticus goes on past ruin to confession and a covenant remembered (vv. 40–45).

notes: **Sevens:** “Seven times” for your sins opens rounds two to five (vv. 18, 21, 24, 28; *sheva'* 4 times). *Qeri*, “contrary,” comes 7 times (vv. 21, 23, 24, 27, 28, 40, 41).

**Abhor:** The verb *ga'al* comes 5 times. The LORD will not abhor his people (v. 11); they abhor his judgments (v. 15); he will abhor them (v. 30); they abhorred his statutes (v. 43); yet he will not abhor them (v. 44).
**Remember:** “Remember” comes 4 times at the end (three in v. 42, once in v. 45): the covenants with Jacob, Abraham and the ancestors, and the land.

The chapter completes the speech opened “in mount Sinai” at 25:1, and v. 46 reads like the close of all the book's laws, the statutes, judgments and laws made “by the hand of Moses.” Chapter 27, on vows, follows as an appendix with its own Sinai closing line (27:34).

**Later echoes:** 2 Chronicles 36:21 says the land lay desolate in the Babylonian exile “until the land had enjoyed her sabbaths,” the threat of vv. 34–35, and Daniel 9:2 reckons its seventy years. Deuteronomy 28 restates the blessings and curses before Israel enters the land.

traditions.text: Before he dies, Lehi tells his sons that the new land is consecrated to those the Lord brings there. If they serve him it will be “a land of liberty unto them”; if iniquity abounds, the land will be cursed for their sakes. His summary, that those who keep the commandments prosper in the land and those who do not are cut off, recurs through the Book of Mormon. Like this chapter, it ties a people's hold on its land to keeping the commandments.

The risen Jesus tells the Nephites that the Father will remember the covenant made with his people, gather them in his own time, and give them again the land of their fathers. Leviticus 26 ends the same way: after the scattering, the LORD remembers his covenant with the patriarchs and remembers the land (vv. 42–45).

After the Saints were driven from Jackson County, Missouri, the Lord says they were slow to hearken, so he was slow to answer their prayers in their trouble. Yet his compassion remains: “I will not utterly cast them off.” The words recall v. 44, where Israel in its enemies' land is neither cast away nor destroyed utterly.

The prophet of the Babylonian exile reuses this chapter more than any other. His promise of a covenant of peace gathers the blessings of vv. 4–13: rain in season, trees and earth yielding fruit, evil beasts gone, safety with none to make them afraid, and the bands of the yoke broken. His oracles of judgment draw on the curses as well, with fathers eating sons and with famine, beasts, pestilence and sword sent together (compare vv. 22–29).

Since v. 3 already speaks of keeping and doing the commandments, the rabbis ask what “walk in my statutes” adds. Their answer: it means to labor in the study of the Torah, with the aim of keeping and doing it. The blessings are thus tied first to study and then to practice.

The rabbis compare v. 19 with Deuteronomy 28:23, where heaven is brass and earth iron. Bronze sweats and iron does not, they reason, so in Deuteronomy the sky still gives a little moisture and the dry ground keeps its fruit. Here the sky is iron and gives nothing, and the earth is bronze and spoils what grows, so this curse is the harsher of the two.

Why are the patriarchs named backward in v. 42, Jacob before Isaac before Abraham? Rashi answers that Jacob, the youngest, is worthy for his children's sake; if not, Isaac stands with him, and if not, Abraham. “Remember” is missing beside Isaac, he says, because the ashes of Isaac, offered on the altar in intent, are always before God.

The Mishnah sets this chapter as the reading for public fast days, and rules that the curses are not to be broken up: one reader reads them all. A teaching in the Talmud adds the passage beginning at v. 14 as one option for the Ninth of Av, the fast for the destroyed temples. The chapter's threat of exile became part of how Jews mourned the exile itself.

Retelling the curses, Philo says the desolate land will at last get its respite and recover its breath, since its people had cast out the seventh-year rests nature taught them. He then turns, like vv. 40–45, to the exiles' return: scattered captives will be freed in one day, and three things will plead for them, God's mercy, the holiness of the nation's founders, and their own reform.

Paul quotes vv. 11–12 to the Corinthians as God's own promise, “I will dwell in them, and walk in them,” and be their God. The tabernacle among Israel becomes the church as the temple of the living God, with no agreement with idols (compare v. 1). Revelation 21:3 uses the same promise for the new Jerusalem, where the tabernacle of God is with men.

In his Dialogue with Trypho, Justin quotes vv. 40–41 in his own Greek-based wording, ending “then shall their uncircumcised heart be turned,” beside Deuteronomy 10:16, where Moses tells Israel to circumcise their hearts. He argues, in sharp polemic, that circumcision of the flesh was given as a sign to set Israel apart, and that what God seeks is the heart. Paul makes the heart point more gently in Romans 2:29.

27.overview:
The book closes with rules for gifts promised to the LORD. A person vowed to the sanctuary is redeemed at a fixed value in silver set by sex and age, from fifty shekels for a man of working age down to three for a baby girl, and the priest lowers it for the poor. A clean animal vowed stays holy and may not be swapped. Unclean animals, houses and fields can be bought back at their value plus a fifth, and fields are priced by the seed they take and the years left before the jubilee. Firstlings already belong to the LORD, things “devoted” can never be redeemed, and a tenth of crops and herds is holy to him.

Almost everything here has a price. The priest's “estimation” runs through the chapter, and buying back a gift costs a fifth more. The exception is the devoted thing of vv. 28–29, which no money can release.

27.hermeneutics:
Promising a god a gift in return for help was ordinary religion in the ancient Near East, and such a promise was a debt. In the Epic of Kirta from Ugarit (tablets of the 13th century BC), King Kirta, marching to win a bride, stops at a shrine of the goddess Athirat (Asherah) and vows her a great gift of gold and silver if his mission succeeds. It succeeds, he fails to pay, and the goddess strikes him with a deadly illness. Leviticus assumes the same seriousness, and Ecclesiastes 5:5 says it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. What the chapter adds is a schedule. A vow of a person, an animal, a house or a field becomes a known amount of silver, scaled down for the poor (v. 8), so the promise can actually be kept.

The “devoted thing” of vv. 28–29 uses the word *cherem*, which also belongs to war. On the Moabite Stone (c. 840 BC), King Mesha boasts that he took the Israelite town of Nebo and killed its seven thousand people because he had devoted them to his god Ashtar-Chemosh, using the same root. Israel's wars knew the same practice (Joshua 6:17–19; 1 Samuel 15:3). That background explains why the devoted thing stands apart from everything else in the chapter. It is not a gift that can be valued and bought back; it is removed from human use for good, and devoted persons “shall surely be put to death” (v. 29).

notes: **The key word:** *Erekh*, “estimation” or valuation, occurs 21 times in the chapter, all of them in vv. 2–27. It falls silent at the devoted thing and the tithe, which are not valued.
**One fifth more:** Redemption costs “the fifth part” added on, 5 times (vv. 13, 15, 19, 27, 31). The verb “redeem” comes 12 times.
**Two endings:** Verse 34 echoes 26:46. Both close with commandments given “in mount Sinai,” so the book has a second ending after the first.

Chapter 26 already sounds like an ending, with its blessings, curses and closing line (26:46). Chapter 27 is an appendix with its own heading (v. 1) and its own Sinai colophon (v. 34), the last verse of the book. It still leans on ch. 25: fields are priced by the years to the jubilee (vv. 17–24), and an unredeemed field goes to the priest at the jubilee (v. 21).
**Links:** Numbers 3:46–47 redeems Israel's surplus firstborn at five shekels each, the value v. 6 sets for a boy under five. Hannah's vow gives Samuel to the LORD for life (1 Samuel 1:11).

traditions.text: Given at Far West, Missouri, the revelation asks the Saints first for their surplus property and then for “one-tenth of all their interest annually,” a standing law for the holy priesthood. Leviticus ends with the tithe of crops and herds as holy to the LORD (vv. 30–32). An earlier revelation had already called the time before the Lord's coming a day of sacrifice and of tithing (D&C 64:23).

The risen Jesus gives the Nephites the words of Malachi, which they did not have: “Will a man rob God?” Israel has robbed him in tithes and offerings, and the Lord promises to open the windows of heaven to those who bring all the tithes into the storehouse. Malachi's charge assumes the tithe laws that begin in vv. 30–32 and continue in Numbers 18.

The law of consecration asks the Saints to consecrate property for the poor “with a covenant and a deed which cannot be broken.” Once laid before the bishop, the properties cannot be taken from the Church, and each member becomes a steward over what he receives. A consecrated gift that cannot be reclaimed parallels the principle of v. 28.

A whole tractate works out vv. 1–8. It opens by ruling that anyone may vow a valuation and anyone may be valued, priests, Levites, Israelites, women and slaves. It separates the fixed “valuation” of the Torah from an “assessment” of a person's market price as a slave, and notes that a child under a month has no valuation, since the scale in v. 6 starts at one month.

Philo restates the values of vv. 3–7 in drachmas and stresses that they ignore beauty, rank and strength, depending only on sex and age. The vow of a great man and a small one weighs the same, he says. A person vowed to God should also not be priced like a slave, whose value rises and falls with the state of his body.

Josephus calls people who dedicate themselves to God a *Corban*, a word he glosses as “gift.” To be freed from that service they pay the priests thirty shekels for a woman and fifty for a man, and if they are too poor, the priests set the sum (v. 8). The same term reappears in Jesus' dispute over vows (below).

The midrash on this chapter tells of four men who made rash vows, among them Jephthah, who promised as a burnt offering whatever first came out of his house (Judges 11:31). It blames him for not having the vow annulled and blames Phinehas the priest for not helping. Resh Lakish holds that Jephthah should have paid money instead; Rabbi Yohanan says the vow never bound him, since a person cannot be offered on the altar.

The Mishnah turns “whatsoever passeth under the rod” (v. 32) into a procedure. The owner drives his animals through a narrow opening one at a time, counts them, and marks every tenth with red paint, saying, This is tithe. Choosing a tenth without counting does not count, since the law forbids picking good or bad (v. 33).

Jesus faults those who let a man declare his goods *Corban*, “a gift” to God, and then refuse to help his father or mother. A dedication to God of the kind Leviticus regulates, he says, has been used to cancel the commandment to honor parents. Josephus's use of the same word (above) shows how familiar the practice was.

Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees tithe even mint, anise and cummin while neglecting the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy and faith. He does not reject the tithe; they ought to have done both, he says. The tithe of “the seed of the land” (v. 30) had been stretched to the smallest garden herbs, while the justice the law aimed at was left undone.

Irenaeus says Christ did not abolish the law's commands but extended them: in place of the law enjoining tithes, he told his followers to share all their possessions with the poor. Elsewhere he contrasts Israel, who had the tithes of their goods consecrated to God, with Christians who have received liberty and set aside all they own for the Lord's purposes, like the widow who gave her whole living.
